meta.name: Meta Ads
meta.intro: Meta Ads Manager holds your spend, delivery and the purchases Meta could link to an ad. It does not know your stock, your margins or what your landing pages say. Most Meta leaks sit in that gap, which is why these playbooks pair it with your store.
meta.connect: Use a Meta Ads connector or MCP server for your assistant if you have one, with read-only access. If not, export a report from Ads Manager (ad, ad set, spend, purchases, link URL, by day) as CSV and upload it.
meta.reads: Spend, results, optimization events, link URLs, delivery by country and placement, account limits.

google.name: Google Ads
google.intro: Google Ads shows what you paid for each search and which conversion actions your campaigns bid toward. The most expensive mistakes are settings, not bids: the wrong conversion goal, or search terms that never sell.
google.connect: Use a Google Ads connector or MCP server with read-only access if you have one. If not, download the campaign, conversion action and search terms reports as CSV and upload them.
google.reads: Campaigns, conversion actions, search terms, spend, account billing.

shopify.name: Shopify
shopify.intro: Shopify is the source of truth for orders, stock, discounts and refunds. Almost every playbook here checks another tool against it, because an ad account or email tool only knows its own side of the sale.
shopify.connect: Use a Shopify connector or MCP server for your assistant with read-only scopes if you have one. If not, export orders, products with inventory, and discounts as CSV from the Shopify admin and upload them.
shopify.reads: Orders, line items, inventory, discount codes, refunds, fulfillment times, shipping zones.

klaviyo.name: Klaviyo
klaviyo.intro: Klaviyo runs the emails that earn money while you sleep: welcome, abandoned cart, browse and win-back flows. They break quietly. A filter change or a paused message can cut flow revenue for weeks before anyone looks.
klaviyo.connect: Use a Klaviyo connector or MCP server with a read-only key if you have one. If not, export flow and campaign performance and sign-up form reports as CSV and upload them.
klaviyo.reads: Flows and messages, sends per message, sign-up forms, lists and segments, back-in-stock requests.

ga4.name: Google Analytics
ga4.intro: Google Analytics shows how people move from landing page to purchase, by channel and device. It is where you tell a site problem from an ad problem: if a step drops on every channel at once, the site changed.
ga4.connect: Use a Google Analytics connector or MCP server with viewer access if you have one. If not, export the funnel, landing page and traffic source reports as CSV and upload them.
ga4.reads: Sessions, funnel steps, landing pages, channels, devices, site search terms.

adlibrary.name: Meta Ad Library

adlibrary.connect: Give your assistant web browsing and the Ad Library search URL for the brand, or paste screenshots and the ads' link URLs into the chat.
adlibrary.reads: Live ads, their copy, offers and dates, start dates, and link URLs.

playbooks.title: Ads optimizing for the wrong goal
playbooks.seo_title: Ads optimizing for the wrong goal? Check with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Check which Google Ads conversion actions and Meta optimization events your sales campaigns bid on, and switch them back to purchases.
playbooks.hook: Your 'sales' campaign might be telling Google that a page view is a sale.
playbooks.answer: Sales campaigns sometimes bid on page views, add-to-cart or sign-ups instead of purchases, because of a primary conversion setting or an ad set event. Connect Google Ads and Meta Ads to Claude, ask it to list each campaign's bidding goal and the spend behind it, then switch sales campaigns to bid on purchases.
playbooks.ask: In Google Ads, list every conversion action marked as primary, and which campaigns use it to bid. In Meta, list the optimization event for every active ad set. Flag any campaign meant to drive sales that is bidding on page views, add-to-cart, sign-ups or anything that is not a purchase. Show the spend going to each.
playbooks.then: Switch those campaigns to bid on purchases. This is usually a one-setting fix.
steps: Connect Google Ads and Meta Ads read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if you use one, or upload conversion settings and campaign exports.
Run the prompt to list primary conversion actions in Google and optimization events in Meta.
Check whether a small account bids on add-to-cart on purpose because it lacks purchase volume.
Switch any sales campaign bidding on a non-purchase event to bid on purchases.
Re-run the check monthly and after any account change.
playbooks.example: 40% of Meta spend went to ad sets optimizing for add-to-cart. Google counted page views as sales.
playbooks.check: Very small accounts sometimes bid on add-to-cart on purpose because there aren't enough purchases. Check that was a choice.

faq.q: Why is my Google Ads campaign counting page views as sales?
faq.a: A page view conversion action is probably marked as primary. Google bids toward every primary conversion, so it treats a page view like a sale.

faq.q: Should my Meta ad sets optimize for add-to-cart?
faq.a: Usually not for sales campaigns. Purchase is the better goal. Very small accounts sometimes choose add-to-cart because they have too few purchases, so check it was a choice.

faq.q: Will this prompt work in other assistants?
faq.a: It will. Any assistant that can read your Google and Meta campaign settings, connected directly or from exported files, can follow the same steps. That includes ChatGPT, Grok and Muse.

faq.q: How hard is the fix?
faq.a: Usually one setting per campaign or ad set. Changing the goal can reset learning, so make the change at a quiet time. Watch results for a week after the switch.

playbooks.title: Ads still running on sold-out products
playbooks.seo_title: Ads running on sold-out products? Find them with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Find Meta and Google ads still sending shoppers to sold-out Shopify products, see the wasted spend, and pause them before more budget goes.
playbooks.hook: You are probably paying Meta to send people to a product they can't buy.
playbooks.answer: Ads keep spending after a product sells out because Meta and Google do not check your Shopify stock. Connect Meta Ads, Google Ads and Shopify to Claude, ask it to match every ad that spent in the last 7 days to its product's stock, and pause the ads pointing at sold-out items. Turn them back on after restock.
playbooks.ask: List every ad that spent money in the last 7 days in Meta and Google. For each one, follow its link to the product in Shopify and check stock across every variant. Show me the ads pointing at products that are sold out, or that will sell out within 7 days at the current sales rate. For each, give the spend since it went out of stock.
playbooks.then: Pause those ads. Turn them back on when the product is restocked. Ask Claude to re-run this every morning.
steps: Connect Meta Ads, Google Ads and Shopify read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if you use one, or upload ad and inventory CSV exports.
Run the prompt to match each ad that spent in the last 7 days to its product's stock across every variant.
Check for pre-order products before acting; they may still sell, so only pause those whose cost per sale has clearly risen.
Pause the ads on sold-out or nearly sold-out products and note them so you can restart them after restock.
Ask Claude to re-run the check every morning.
playbooks.example: 6 ads were still pointing at a sold-out bestseller. $1,400 spent in 5 days, 2 orders.
playbooks.check: If the product takes pre-orders, it may still sell. Only pause when cost per sale has clearly risen.

faq.q: Why do my ads keep running when a product is out of stock?
faq.a: Ad platforms do not read your store's inventory by default. An ad keeps its budget and keeps sending clicks to the product page until someone pauses it, even when every variant shows sold out.

faq.q: Does this work with ChatGPT or other assistants?
faq.a: Yes. The prompt works in any assistant that can read your ad and Shopify data, whether through a live connection or exported CSV files. ChatGPT, Grok or Muse can run the same match if you give them the same reports.

faq.q: Is it safe to give Claude access to my ad account?
faq.a: Use read-only access. Claude only needs to see ads, spend and links to find the problem. You pause the ads yourself, so nothing changes in your account unless you change it.

faq.q: What about products that are only low on stock?
faq.a: The prompt also flags products likely to sell out within 7 days at the current sales rate. That gives you time to cut budget or restock before the ad starts wasting money.

playbooks.title: Your email domain isn't authenticated
playbooks.seo_title: No DMARC record? Check your email domain with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Check whether your sending domain has SPF, DKIM and DMARC, learn what Gmail and Yahoo require from bulk senders, and fix what is missing.
playbooks.hook: No DMARC record means Gmail may be sending your emails to spam. It takes 10 seconds to check.
playbooks.answer: Marketing emails can land in spam when the sending domain lacks SPF, DKIM or DMARC, which Gmail and Yahoo now expect from bulk senders. Ask Claude to look up your sending domain's public DNS records and explain what is missing. No login is needed. Add the missing records with whoever runs your domain, starting DMARC at p=none.
playbooks.ask: Look up the public DNS records for [your sending domain]. Do I have SPF, DKIM and DMARC set up? Is DMARC set to none, quarantine or reject? Explain in plain words what's missing and what Gmail and Yahoo now require from bulk senders.
playbooks.then: Add the missing records with whoever runs your domain. Start DMARC at p=none, then tighten.
steps: Find the domain your emails actually send from; it may be a subdomain. A public DNS lookup needs no login.
Ask Claude to run the prompt with web search or a DNS lookup tool, or paste in DNS records you looked up.
Confirm you checked the sending subdomain, not just your main domain.
Add missing SPF, DKIM or DMARC records with whoever runs your domain, starting DMARC at p=none.
Re-check after the change, then quarterly.
playbooks.example: The sending domain had no DMARC record at all.
playbooks.check: Check the domain your emails actually send from. It may be a subdomain, not your main one.

faq.q: What is DMARC and do I need it?
faq.a: DMARC is a DNS record that tells inbox providers how to treat mail that fails SPF or DKIM checks. Gmail and Yahoo expect bulk senders to have one.

faq.q: What DMARC policy should I start with?
faq.a: Start with p=none to watch reports without blocking mail. Move to quarantine, then reject, once you know all your real senders pass. Moving too fast can block your own mail.

faq.q: Can ChatGPT check my DMARC record?
faq.a: Yes, if it can look up DNS or browse the web. Any assistant that can read public DNS records, or that you paste the records into, can follow this prompt.

faq.q: Which domain should I check?
faq.a: The one in your emails' from address and sending setup. Email tools often send from a subdomain, which needs its own records. Check that subdomain too.

playbooks.title: Sign-up popup stopped working
playbooks.seo_title: Email sign-ups dropped? Check your popup with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: See whether a sign-up drop came from your popup, its offer or traffic by charting Klaviyo sign-ups against GA4 sessions and Shopify code orders.
playbooks.hook: Email sign-ups halving overnight is rarely a traffic problem.
playbooks.answer: When email sign-ups fall sharply while site traffic holds steady, the popup usually broke or its offer changed. Connect Klaviyo, Google Analytics and Shopify to Claude, ask it to chart daily sign-ups against sessions for 90 days, and check the form, its offer and welcome-code orders. Restore the popup and test it yourself.
playbooks.ask: Chart email sign-ups per day for the last 90 days next to site sessions per day. Flag any day sign-ups fell by more than 40% while sessions held steady. Then check: is the popup form still live, did its offer change, and are welcome-code orders in Shopify falling at the same time?
playbooks.then: Restore the popup or its offer. Sign up yourself with a test address to check the code arrives and applies at checkout.
steps: Connect Klaviyo, Google Analytics and Shopify read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if available, or upload sign-up, session and order exports.
Run the prompt to chart daily sign-ups next to sessions and flag sudden drops.
Ask whether someone changed the popup on purpose; then the finding is the cost of that choice.
Restore the popup or its offer, then sign up with a test address to confirm the code arrives and works.
Re-run the check weekly.
playbooks.example: The popup switched from 10% off to a giveaway on 3 Oct. Sign-ups fell 55% and welcome-code orders fell with them.
playbooks.check: If someone changed the popup on purpose, the finding is 'here is what that choice costs', not 'it broke'.

faq.q: Why did my email sign-ups suddenly drop?
faq.a: If traffic stayed the same, the popup likely stopped showing, broke on some devices, or its offer changed. A weaker offer can cut sign-ups even when the form works.

faq.q: How do I test my sign-up popup?
faq.a: Sign up yourself with a test email address. Check that the welcome email arrives and that the code applies at checkout. Try it on a phone and a desktop, since a popup can break on one and not the other.

faq.q: Can other assistants run this prompt?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can read the same sign-up, session and order data, connected or from an uploaded file, can follow it. That includes ChatGPT, Grok and Muse.

faq.q: What if we changed the popup on purpose?
faq.a: Then nothing is broken. The useful output is what the change cost in sign-ups and welcome-code orders, so you can decide whether to keep it.

playbooks.title: An email flow quietly stopped sending
playbooks.seo_title: Klaviyo flow stopped sending? Find it with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Find Klaviyo flow emails whose sends dropped to zero or halved, see the revenue lost, and fix the broken message or filter.
playbooks.hook: Your abandoned-cart email can break and nobody notices for weeks.
playbooks.answer: A Klaviyo flow can stop sending after an edit, a broken filter or an accidental pause, and nothing alerts you. Connect Klaviyo to Claude and ask it to chart weekly sends for every live flow message over 12 weeks. It flags drops to zero, big falls and flows that never sent. Fix the message or filter, then rebuild paused flows.
playbooks.ask: For every live flow in Klaviyo, show emails sent per week for the last 12 weeks, message by message. Flag any message whose sends dropped to zero or fell by more than half, any live flow that has never sent, and any flow that was paused or replaced. Show the revenue each one made before and after.
playbooks.then: Fix the broken message or filter. Rebuild any flow that was paused by accident. This is often a 30-minute fix.
steps: Connect Klaviyo read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if available, or upload flow performance exports.
Run the prompt to chart weekly sends per flow message for the last 12 weeks.
Compare sends with checkout starts; if traffic fell, sends fall too and nothing is broken.
Fix the broken message or filter, and rebuild any flow paused by accident.
Ask Claude to re-run the check weekly.
playbooks.example: The second email in the cart flow stopped sending on 12 Oct. Flow revenue fell 70% in a month.
playbooks.check: If traffic fell, sends fall too. Compare sends with the number of people who started a checkout.

faq.q: Why did my Klaviyo flow stop sending?
faq.a: Common causes are an edited trigger, a filter that now excludes everyone, a message set to draft, or a flow that was paused or replaced. The sends chart shows exactly when it stopped.

faq.q: How do I know it is broken and not just low traffic?
faq.a: Compare flow sends with the number of people who started a checkout. If checkouts held steady while sends fell, the flow is the problem. If both fell together, look at traffic instead.

faq.q: Can ChatGPT or Grok run this check?
faq.a: Yes. Give any assistant your Klaviyo flow data, through a connection or an exported file, and the same prompt finds the drop. ChatGPT, Grok and Muse all handle this kind of weekly send data well.

faq.q: Is it safe to connect Klaviyo to Claude?
faq.a: Use read-only access. Claude only needs send and revenue numbers. You make any fix inside Klaviyo yourself. Read access is enough to chart sends and spot a drop, so there is no need for edit rights.

playbooks.title: Purchases stopped recording in your ad account
playbooks.seo_title: Meta not tracking purchases? Check it against Shopify
playbooks.meta_description: Compare Meta purchases with Shopify orders day by day to see when tracking broke, how long it has been down, and what to check first.
playbooks.hook: Your ads can look like they stopped working when really your tracking did.
playbooks.answer: When Meta suddenly shows few or zero purchases while Shopify still has orders, tracking usually broke, not the ads. Connect Meta Ads and Shopify to Claude and ask it to compare daily purchases with daily orders for 30 days. A sudden change in the ratio shows the start date. Then check the pixel and the Shopify channel connection.
playbooks.ask: For each of the last 30 days, compare the purchases Meta recorded with the orders Shopify recorded. Work out the usual ratio. Flag any day where Meta recorded zero purchases while Shopify had orders, and any day the ratio moved more than 30% away from normal. Tell me when it started.
playbooks.then: If purchases dropped to zero, check the pixel and the Shopify channel connection right away: Meta is now bidding blind.
steps: Connect Meta Ads and Shopify read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if available, or upload daily purchase and order exports.
Run the prompt to compare Meta purchases with Shopify orders for each of the last 30 days.
Remember Meta always counts fewer orders than Shopify; look for a sudden ratio change, not the normal gap.
If purchases dropped to zero, check the pixel and the Shopify sales channel connection right away.
Ask Claude to re-run the comparison every day.
playbooks.example: Meta recorded 0 purchases for 4 days while $3,000 was spent. Shopify had 140 orders.
playbooks.check: Meta only counts orders it can link to an ad, so it is always below Shopify. Look for a sudden change in the ratio, not the gap itself.

faq.q: Why is Meta showing zero purchases when I have orders?
faq.a: Usually the pixel or the Shopify connection to Meta stopped sending purchase events. A theme change, app update or expired channel connection can cause it. Meta then bids without sales data.

faq.q: Is it normal for Meta to show fewer sales than Shopify?
faq.a: Yes. Meta only counts orders it can link to an ad, so its number is always lower. What matters is a sudden change in the ratio between the two, which points to a tracking break.

faq.q: Can I run this with Grok or ChatGPT instead of Claude?
faq.a: You can. Any assistant that can read your daily Meta purchases and Shopify orders, either connected or from exported files, can follow the same prompt and spot the change.

faq.q: How fast should I fix broken tracking?
faq.a: Right away. While purchases are not recorded, Meta's bidding has no sales signal, so spend can drift toward people who do not buy. Every day you wait adds spend.

playbooks.title: The ad says one thing, the page says another
playbooks.seo_title: Ad price doesn't match the landing page? Check with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Compare every live Meta ad's price, offer and product with the page it links to on a phone, and find the gaps that cost you clicks.
playbooks.hook: Your ad says $45. The page it links to says $60. Every click lands on that gap.
playbooks.answer: Ad and page mismatches usually come from a price change, an ended offer or a swapped product that never reached the ad. Give Claude web browsing and have it list every active ad in the Meta Ad Library, open each link on a phone-sized browser, and compare. Then make the page match, or repoint the ad.
playbooks.ask: Open the Meta Ad Library for [brand] and list every active ad. For each one, write down the price, discount, free-shipping promise and product shown. Then open each ad's link on a phone-sized browser and note what the page and cart actually show. List every mismatch: price, offer, product, colour or stock.
playbooks.then: Make the page match the ad, or point the ad at a page that does.
steps: Give Claude web browsing, or paste your Meta Ad Library results and landing page links into the chat. No login is needed.
Run the prompt for your brand so Claude lists every active ad with its price, offer, shipping promise and product.
Have Claude open each ad's link on a phone-sized browser and add the item to the cart.
Rule out planned differences, like bundle pricing or first-order discounts that only show in the cart.
Fix each real mismatch: update the page, or point the ad at a page that matches it.
Re-run the check every week, and after any price change or new offer.
playbooks.example: The ad promised $45. The landing page showed $60 in three places.
playbooks.check: Some prices change at checkout on purpose (bundles, first-order discounts). Check the cart, not just the page.

faq.q: Why does a mismatch between the ad and the page hurt sales?
faq.a: It breaks the promise that earned the click. A shopper who expects $45 and sees $60 often leaves, and you still paid for the visit. Smaller gaps in offer, color or shipping terms cause the same loss of trust.

faq.q: Do I need access to my ad account?
faq.a: No. The Meta Ad Library is public and shows every active ad for any page. Claude only needs a web browser, or you can paste the ads and their links into the chat yourself.

faq.q: Can I run this with ChatGPT or another assistant?
faq.a: Yes. The prompt works in any assistant that can browse the web, such as ChatGPT, Grok or Muse. If yours cannot browse, paste in the ad text and page details and ask the same question.

faq.q: What counts as a mismatch?
faq.a: Any difference a shopper would notice between the ad and what they see after clicking: price, discount, free-shipping promise, product, color or stock. Check the cart too, since some prices change there on purpose.

playbooks.title: Lapsed customers nobody emails
playbooks.seo_title: Lapsed customers nobody emails? Win them back with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Count past buyers who haven't ordered in six months, see how many are still subscribed, and set up a win-back flow you can measure.
playbooks.hook: Thousands of your past buyers haven't ordered in 6 months, and nobody's asking them back.
playbooks.answer: Lapsed buyers often go unemailed because no win-back flow exists. Connect Shopify and Klaviyo to Claude and ask how many buyers have not ordered in six months, how many are still subscribed, and whether any flow targets them. Then build a win-back flow and hold back a small random slice to measure what it adds.
playbooks.ask: How many customers bought at least once but haven't ordered in 6 months? How many of them are still subscribed to email? Is any flow or campaign aimed at them? Show the size of the group and what a 2% return rate would be worth at my average order value.
playbooks.then: Set up a win-back flow. Hold back a small random slice so you can count what it really added.
steps: Connect Shopify and Klaviyo to Claude read-only, through a connector or MCP server if available, or upload a Shopify customer export and a Klaviyo list of flows.
Run the prompt to size the lapsed group, see who is still subscribed, and estimate what a small return rate is worth.
Count only customers who are still opted in to email.
Build a win-back flow, and hold back a small random slice who do not get it.
Re-run monthly and compare the flow's group with the held-back slice.
playbooks.example: 1,800 past buyers hadn't ordered in 6 months. None got a win-back email.
playbooks.check: Count only people who are still opted in, and measure against the held-back slice.

faq.q: How long before a customer counts as lapsed?
faq.a: The playbook uses six months without an order. Adjust that to how often people normally rebuy what you sell. A product people use up quickly may need a shorter window.

faq.q: Why hold back a slice of customers?
faq.a: Some lapsed buyers would come back anyway. A small random group that gets no win-back email shows how many return on their own, so you can count what the flow really added.

faq.q: Can another AI assistant do this?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can read your Shopify customers and Klaviyo flows, such as ChatGPT, Grok or Muse, can answer the same prompt. Exported files work if it has no live connection.

faq.q: What should a win-back email say?
faq.a: Remind them what they bought, show what is new or related, and give one clear reason to come back. A discount is optional, so try a version without one first and compare.

playbooks.title: Treat every launch and restock as a reason to email past buyers
playbooks.seo_title: Email past buyers on every launch and restock, with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Compare repeat orders in launch weeks with normal weeks, check whether past buyers heard about recent drops, and email them on every launch.
playbooks.hook: Past buyers buy again in launch weeks. Make sure they hear about every launch.
playbooks.answer: Past buyers tend to reorder in launch and restock weeks, but often never hear about the drop. Connect Shopify and Klaviyo to Claude and ask it to compare repeat orders in launch weeks with normal weeks, then check whether matching past buyers were emailed about the last five drops. Email them every time, matched to what they bought.
playbooks.ask: Compare repeat orders per week in launch or restock weeks with normal weeks over the last 12 months. Then list the last 5 launches or restocks and whether past buyers of that size, style or category were emailed about each.
playbooks.then: Email past buyers on every drop, matched to what they bought before.
steps: Connect Shopify and Klaviyo to Claude read-only, through connectors or MCP servers if available, or upload a Shopify orders export and a Klaviyo campaign list.
Run the prompt so Claude compares repeat orders in launch weeks with normal weeks.
Compare with weeks that had a promo but no launch, so other offers don't explain the lift.
Build segments of past buyers by size, style or category, and email them on every drop.
Re-run the check after each launch.
playbooks.example: Repeat orders ran 1.5 to 5 times normal in launch weeks.
playbooks.check: Launch weeks often include other promos. Compare with weeks that had a promo but no launch.

faq.q: Why email past buyers about launches?
faq.a: They already know and trust your products, and a launch gives them a fresh reason to buy. The check shows whether your launch weeks actually lift repeat orders for your store.

faq.q: How do I match buyers to a launch?
faq.a: Use what they bought before: the same size, style or category as the new product or restock. Shopify order history holds this, and Klaviyo can build segments from it.

faq.q: Does this work with other AI assistants?
faq.a: Yes. ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can read your Shopify orders and Klaviyo campaigns, live or from exports, can run the same prompt and give the same comparison.

faq.q: What if launch weeks also had promos?
faq.a: Then the promo may explain the lift. Compare with weeks that had a promo but no launch to separate the two effects before you decide how much the launch email matters.

playbooks.title: Shift spend before your hero product sells out
playbooks.seo_title: Move ad spend before products sell out, using Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Project which top products sell out before your peak at last year's pace, see the ad spend on each, and move budget to stock that lasts.
playbooks.hook: Spending hard on a product that'll sell out before Black Friday is paying to run out early.
playbooks.answer: Spending hard on a product that will sell out before peak season pays to run out early. Connect Shopify, Meta Ads and Google Ads to Claude and ask it to project stock for your top ten products at last year's peak pace, show spend on each, and suggest where to move budget. Reorder the products that won't last.
playbooks.ask: For my top 10 products, take current stock and the sales rate over the last 14 days. At last year's peak-season pace, which products sell out before [date]? For each, show how much ad spend points at it. Suggest which products to move spend toward.
playbooks.then: Move spend toward products with stock to last the peak. Order more of the ones that won't.
steps: Connect Shopify, Meta Ads and Google Ads to Claude read-only, through connectors or MCP servers if available, or upload inventory, sales and ad spend exports.
Run the prompt with your peak date so Claude projects which top products sell out first.
Use last year's peak-week pace, not this month's average. Peak weeks can run several times normal orders.
Move spend toward products with enough stock, and place reorders for the ones that won't last.
Re-run weekly in the run-up to a peak.
playbooks.example: 3 top sellers would sell out by 20 Nov at last year's Black Friday pace.
playbooks.check: Peak weeks can run 3 to 4 times normal orders. Use last year's peak, not this month's average.

faq.q: Why use last year's peak pace instead of current sales?
faq.a: Peak weeks can run three to four times normal orders. A forecast built on this month's average can say you have plenty of stock when you may sell out within days of the peak starting.

faq.q: What if this product didn't exist last peak season?
faq.a: Use a similar product's peak pace, or apply your store-wide peak lift to the product's current sales rate. Treat the result as a rough range, not an exact date.

faq.q: Will the same prompt work in ChatGPT?
faq.a: Yes. ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can read your Shopify inventory and ad spend, live or from uploaded files, can run it and give the same projection.

faq.q: Should I stop ads on products that will sell out?
faq.a: Not always. Lower spend so stock lasts through the peak, and keep some coverage if a reorder will arrive in time. The goal is to have stock on the days that matter most.

playbooks.title: A flow filter skips real shoppers
playbooks.seo_title: Abandoned cart email not sending? Check filters with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Compare Shopify checkout starts with Klaviyo flow entries to see how many shoppers miss your abandoned-checkout email, and which filter skips them.
playbooks.hook: 1,400 people started checkout last week. How many got your email?
playbooks.answer: When few shoppers get your abandoned-checkout email, a flow filter is often skipping them, such as a rule that excludes anyone who ever ordered. Connect Shopify and Klaviyo to Claude and ask it to compare checkout starts with flow entries and first-email sends. If fewer than half get it, Claude names the rule to loosen or fix.
playbooks.ask: How many people started a checkout last week in Shopify? How many of them entered my abandoned-checkout flow in Klaviyo, and how many got the first email? If fewer than half got it, show me the flow's trigger and filters and tell me which rule is excluding them.
playbooks.then: Loosen or fix the filter. A common cause is a 'has placed an order ever' rule that skips every past customer.
steps: Connect Shopify and Klaviyo read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if you have one, or upload checkout and flow exports.
Run the prompt to compare last week's checkout starts with flow entries and first-email sends.
Count only shoppers who never finished; people who bought within the hour should be skipped.
Loosen or fix the filter that excludes real shoppers, such as a 'has placed an order ever' rule.
Re-run the check monthly.
playbooks.example: 1,400 started checkout. 90 got the first email.
playbooks.check: People who bought within the hour should be skipped. Count only those who never finished.

faq.q: Why are so few people getting my abandoned cart email?
faq.a: A trigger or flow filter is usually excluding them. A rule that skips anyone who has ever placed an order removes every past customer from the flow.

faq.q: Should people who already bought get the email?
faq.a: No. Anyone who finished the order within the hour should be skipped. The count that matters is shoppers who started checkout and never bought. Those people need the email most.

faq.q: Does this prompt need Claude?
faq.a: No. ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant with access to your Shopify checkouts and Klaviyo flow numbers, live or exported, can run it. The method is the same in each.

faq.q: How often should I check my flow filters?
faq.a: Monthly, and after any edit to the flow. Filters change quietly when someone copies or rebuilds a flow. A quick monthly check catches a bad filter before it costs a full quarter of recovered carts.

playbooks.title: Ad sets spending with no sales
playbooks.seo_title: Ad sets spending with no sales? Find them with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: List Meta and TikTok ad sets that spent several times your normal cost per sale with zero purchases, then pause or cut them.
playbooks.hook: One ad set can quietly spend three times your normal cost per sale and sell nothing.
playbooks.answer: Some ad sets keep spending for weeks without a sale because nobody checks them against the account's normal cost per purchase. Connect Meta Ads or TikTok Ads to Claude, ask it to find ad sets that spent more than 3 times your average cost per purchase in 14 days with no purchases, then pause them or move the budget.
playbooks.ask: Work out my average cost per purchase over the last 30 days. Then list every ad set that has spent more than 3 times that amount in the last 14 days with zero purchases. Sort by spend.
playbooks.then: Pause them or cut their budget. Move the money to the ad sets that are selling.
steps: Connect Meta Ads and TikTok Ads read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if available, or upload ad set performance exports.
Run the prompt to find ad sets over 3 times your average cost per purchase with zero purchases.
Confirm tracking works first, and skip new ad sets in their first 3 days.
Pause the flagged ad sets or cut their budget, and move the money to ad sets that sell.
Ask Claude to re-run this twice a week.
playbooks.example: One ad set spent $1,200 with no sales. The account's usual cost per sale is $40.
playbooks.check: Make sure tracking is working first (see the playbook above). A new ad set in its first 3 days may not have had time.

faq.q: How long should I let an ad set run with no sales?
faq.a: A common rule is to act once it has spent about 3 times your normal cost per purchase with no sales. New ad sets get a few days to settle before you judge them.

faq.q: What if my tracking is broken?
faq.a: Then every ad set can look like it has no sales. Check that purchases are being recorded before pausing anything. A broken pixel makes good ad sets look bad, and pausing them would cut real sales.

faq.q: Can I use ChatGPT for this?
faq.a: Yes. The prompt works with ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can see your ad set spend and purchases, live or through an exported report.

faq.q: Is it safe to connect my ad account?
faq.a: Give read-only access. Claude only reads spend and results. You make the pause or budget change yourself. Read access is enough to find the ad sets that spend without selling.

playbooks.title: Ads shown where you don't ship
playbooks.seo_title: Ads shown where you don't ship? Find them with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Compare your Shopify shipping countries with Meta spend by country to find ad sets showing ads where you cannot deliver, then restrict them.
playbooks.hook: Some of your ad budget is probably going to countries you can't deliver to.
playbooks.answer: Ad sets can show ads in countries your store does not ship to when targeting is broad or set to worldwide. Connect Meta Ads and Shopify to Claude and ask it to compare your shipping countries with 30 days of Meta spend by country. It names the ad sets spending where you cannot deliver. Restrict those ad sets.
playbooks.ask: List the countries my Shopify store ships to. Then break down my Meta spend for the last 30 days by country. Show any spend in countries I don't ship to, and the ad sets responsible.
playbooks.then: Restrict those ad sets to countries you ship to.
steps: Connect Meta Ads and Shopify read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if you have one, or upload a spend-by-country report and your shipping zones.
Run the prompt to compare spend by country with the countries you ship to.
Check whether any brand-awareness campaigns target worldwide on purpose.
Restrict the flagged ad sets to countries you ship to.
Re-run the check monthly.
playbooks.example: $400 went to ads shown in countries the store doesn't ship to.
playbooks.check: Brand-awareness campaigns may be global on purpose.

faq.q: Why are my Meta ads showing in other countries?
faq.a: Targeting may be broad, set to worldwide, or include regions you added once and forgot. Advantage audience options can also widen reach. A broken shipping zone setting in Shopify can also cause a mismatch.

faq.q: How do I see Meta spend by country?
faq.a: Break down an ad report by country in Ads Manager, or ask Claude to pull it. Then compare it with the shipping zones in Shopify.

faq.q: Can Grok or ChatGPT do this instead?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can read your Meta spend by country and Shopify shipping zones, connected or as uploaded files, can run this prompt. The data is the same, so the result is too.

faq.q: Is spend outside my shipping area always wasted?
faq.a: For sales campaigns, yes. Brand-awareness campaigns may run globally on purpose, so check before restricting them. A shopper in a country you cannot deliver to cannot buy, so every click there is lost money.

playbooks.title: Ads about to stop for billing
playbooks.seo_title: All ads stopped at once? Check billing with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Check Meta, Google and TikTok ad accounts for spending limits, failed payments and expiring cards before your ads stop running.
playbooks.hook: Every ad stopping at once is usually a card or a spending limit, not the algorithm.
playbooks.answer: When every ad stops at once, the cause is usually an account spending limit, a failed payment or an expired card, not the algorithm. Connect Meta Ads, Google Ads and TikTok Ads to Claude and ask it to check limits and payment methods, estimate when each limit runs out at current spend, and flag sudden spend drops.
playbooks.ask: Check every ad account for an account spending limit, a failed payment, or a payment method expiring soon. At the current daily spend, when does each limit run out? Also flag any day in the last 30 where total spend dropped below 20% of normal.
playbooks.then: Raise the limit or update the card before it runs out.
steps: Connect Meta Ads, Google Ads and TikTok Ads read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if available, or upload billing and daily spend reports.
Run the prompt to check spending limits, failed payments and expiring cards in every account.
Ask whether anyone paused ads on purpose before treating a spend drop as a problem.
Raise the limit or update the card before it runs out.
Ask Claude to re-run the check every day.
playbooks.example: The Meta spending limit runs out in 2 days at the current rate.
playbooks.check: A planned pause looks the same. Ask whether anyone paused on purpose.

faq.q: Why did all my ads stop running at the same time?
faq.a: Usually an account spending limit was reached, a payment failed, or a card expired. These stop every campaign in the account at once. Check billing settings before you change any targeting or creative.

faq.q: How do I know when my spending limit will run out?
faq.a: Divide the remaining limit by your current daily spend. The prompt does this for each account so you see the date ahead of time. Then you can raise the limit or add funds before the ads go dark.

faq.q: Can I use this prompt with ChatGPT?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can see your ad accounts' billing and spend, connected or from exported reports, can run the same check. ChatGPT, Grok and Muse can all follow it with the same inputs.

faq.q: Is it safe to give Claude billing access?
faq.a: Use read-only access and never share card numbers. Claude only needs limits, payment status and spend. You update payment details yourself. Card details are never needed to run the check.

playbooks.title: Search terms that never sell
playbooks.seo_title: Google Ads search terms not converting? Fix with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Find Google Ads search terms that spent money with no conversions, group them into themes, and add negative keywords to stop the waste.
playbooks.hook: Open your Google Ads search terms report. Some of what you pay for is embarrassing.
playbooks.answer: Broad and phrase match keywords pull in search terms that never sell, and the waste stays hidden unless you read the search terms report. Connect Google Ads to Claude and ask it to list 90 days of terms that spent more than twice your cost per sale with no conversions, grouped by theme. Add the suggested negative keywords.
playbooks.ask: Pull the search terms report for the last 90 days. List every search term that spent more than [2x my cost per sale] with no conversions. Group them into themes, and suggest negative keywords for each theme.
playbooks.then: Add the negatives. Re-run monthly; new junk terms keep appearing.
steps: Connect Google Ads read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if available, or upload a 90-day search terms report.
Run the prompt with your own cost per sale filled in.
Confirm conversion tracking worked for the whole period before trusting the zero-conversion list.
Review the themes and add the negative keywords that fit.
Re-run the report monthly; new junk terms keep appearing.
playbooks.example: $2,100 a month went to search terms that never sold.
playbooks.check: Check that conversion tracking was working for the whole period.

faq.q: How do I find wasted spend in Google Ads?
faq.a: Open the search terms report and look for terms with spend and no conversions. The prompt filters and groups them so the waste is easy to see.

faq.q: What spend threshold should I use?
faq.a: A common line is twice your normal cost per sale with no conversions. Below that, a term may not have had enough clicks to judge.

faq.q: Does this work with ChatGPT or Muse?
faq.a: Yes. Upload the search terms report or connect Google Ads to any assistant that can read it, and the same prompt applies. ChatGPT, Grok and Muse all handle this kind of report.

faq.q: Will negative keywords block good traffic?
faq.a: They can if too broad. Review each theme before adding it, and keep negatives specific to the junk terms. A term like a product name plus a typo may still sell, so check it before you block it.

playbooks.title: Purchases counted twice
playbooks.seo_title: Meta counting purchases twice? Check ROAS with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Find out whether Meta counts each order twice by comparing its purchases with Shopify orders, and learn which duplicate event to remove.
playbooks.hook: If your ROAS looks too good to be true, check whether each order counts twice.
playbooks.answer: If Meta records more purchases than Shopify has orders, the purchase event is likely firing twice, often from two pixels or two apps on the thank-you page. Connect Meta Ads and Shopify to Claude, ask it to list days where Meta's count beats Shopify's, and check $0, replacement and renewal orders. Then remove the duplicate event.
playbooks.ask: Compare Meta's recorded purchases with Shopify orders for the last 30 days. If Meta records more purchases than Shopify has orders on any day, list those days. Then check whether $0 orders, replacement orders or subscription renewals are firing purchase events.
playbooks.then: Fix the duplicate event (usually two pixels or two apps firing Purchase on the thank-you page). Your real cost per sale is higher than you think.
steps: Connect Meta Ads and Shopify read-only, via a Claude connector or MCP server if you have one, or upload 30 days of purchase and order exports.
Run the prompt to list days where Meta recorded more purchases than Shopify orders.
Recount after removing $0, replacement and subscription renewal orders, since those inflate counts without a pixel bug.
Find and remove the duplicate Purchase event, usually a second pixel or app on the thank-you page.
Re-run the check weekly to confirm the counts line up.
playbooks.example: Meta counted 1.6 purchases for every real order. The purchase event fired twice on the thank-you page.
playbooks.check: Recount after removing $0 and replacement orders. Those inflate the count without being a pixel bug.

faq.q: Why does Meta show more purchases than I have orders?
faq.a: The purchase event is usually firing more than once per order. Two pixels, two apps or a manual code snippet plus an app on the thank-you page are common causes.

faq.q: How does double counting affect my ROAS?
faq.a: It makes ROAS look higher than it is. Your real cost per sale is higher than the report shows, so budget decisions based on it can overspend.

faq.q: Does the prompt work outside Claude?
faq.a: Yes. ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can read the same Meta and Shopify numbers, connected or as uploaded files, can run this comparison.

faq.q: Do $0 orders count as purchases in Meta?
faq.a: They can. Free replacement orders and some subscription renewals can fire purchase events. Remove them from the count before deciding the pixel is broken. Then compare again.

playbooks.title: Products turned down in Google Shopping
playbooks.seo_title: Products disapproved in Merchant Center? Fix with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: List disapproved and limited Merchant Center products, match them to Shopify sales, and fix the disapprovals that cost the most revenue first.
playbooks.hook: Your bestsellers might be invisible in Google Shopping, and the reason is in a report nobody opens.
playbooks.answer: Products get disapproved or limited in Google Shopping for reasons like missing GTINs, price mismatches or image problems, and bestsellers can disappear without notice. Connect Merchant Center and Shopify to Claude and ask it to rank disapproved products by 90-day Shopify revenue. Fix the top reasons first, starting with in-stock items.
playbooks.ask: In Merchant Center, list every product that is disapproved or limited, with the reason. Match each one to its Shopify sales over the last 90 days and sort by revenue, so I can see which disapprovals hurt most.
playbooks.then: Fix the top reasons first (usually missing GTIN, price mismatch or image problems).
steps: Connect Merchant Center and Shopify read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if you have one, or upload a diagnostics report and sales export.
Run the prompt to list disapproved or limited products and sort them by Shopify revenue.
Filter out products you no longer sell; only in-stock items matter.
Fix the top reasons first, usually missing GTIN, price mismatch or image problems.
Ask Claude to re-run the check weekly.
playbooks.example: 38 products turned down, including 4 of the top 10 sellers.
playbooks.check: Products you've stopped selling don't matter. Filter to items in stock.

faq.q: Why are my products disapproved in Google Merchant Center?
faq.a: Common reasons are missing GTINs, a price on the feed that does not match the site, image problems, or policy issues. Merchant Center shows the reason for each item.

faq.q: Which disapprovals should I fix first?
faq.a: Fix the products that earn the most in Shopify. Ranking by revenue shows which fixes bring back the most sales. A disapproved bestseller costs far more than a disapproved slow seller, so start at the top of the list.

faq.q: Does this need Claude, or will Grok work?
faq.a: Grok, ChatGPT, Muse or any assistant that can read your Merchant Center report and Shopify sales, whether connected or uploaded, can run it. The steps stay the same.

faq.q: How often do disapprovals happen?
faq.a: They can appear any time a feed or policy changes. A weekly check catches them before a bestseller is missing for long. Feed apps and price changes are common triggers.

playbooks.title: A discount code stopped working
playbooks.seo_title: Discount code stopped working? Find out why with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Spot Shopify discount codes whose weekly orders collapsed, check whether they expired or hit a limit, and fix the emails that still promise them.
playbooks.hook: Your best discount code can die on a Tuesday and nobody gets an alert.
playbooks.answer: A discount code can stop working when it expires, hits a usage limit or gets edited, and Shopify sends no alert. Connect Shopify and Klaviyo to Claude and ask it to chart weekly orders for your top 10 codes over 6 months. It flags sharp drops and why. Re-enable or replace the code and update emails that promise it.
playbooks.ask: List my top 10 discount codes by orders over the last 6 months. For each, show orders per week. Flag any code whose weekly orders fell by more than 70% compared with its usual level, and check whether it expired, hit a usage limit or was edited.
playbooks.then: Re-enable or replace the code. Update any emails or popups that still promise it.
steps: Connect Shopify and Klaviyo read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if you use one, or upload discount and order exports.
Run the prompt to chart weekly orders for your top 10 discount codes.
Skip codes that ended on purpose with a campaign; only flag codes still promised somewhere live.
Re-enable or replace broken codes, and update any emails or popups that still promise them.
Ask Claude to re-run the check weekly.
playbooks.example: WELCOME10 brought 60 orders a week until 12 Oct. Now it brings 2.
playbooks.check: Codes tied to one campaign end on purpose. Only flag codes still promised somewhere live.

faq.q: Why did my Shopify discount code stop working?
faq.a: The most common reasons are an end date, a usage limit, or an edit to its rules, such as a new minimum order. Shopify does not notify you when this happens.

faq.q: How do I find codes promised in my emails?
faq.a: Ask Claude to search your live Klaviyo flows and forms for the code. Any email that still promises a dead code frustrates shoppers at checkout.

faq.q: Do I need Claude for this?
faq.a: No. ChatGPT, Grok or Muse can run the same prompt if they can read your Shopify discount orders and Klaviyo content, either connected or from exports.

faq.q: Is it safe to connect Shopify?
faq.a: Use read-only access. Claude reads orders and discount settings. You change the code yourself in Shopify. Nothing changes in your store unless you change it. Read access is enough to find a dead code and see why it stopped.

playbooks.title: Orders stuck unshipped
playbooks.seo_title: Shopify orders stuck unshipped? Find them with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: List paid Shopify orders older than 3 days that have not shipped and chart weekly time to ship, so you clear the backlog before complaints start.
playbooks.hook: Late orders turn into refunds, chargebacks and one-star reviews.
playbooks.answer: Paid orders can sit unshipped because of stock gaps, address issues or a slow warehouse, and late orders turn into refunds and bad reviews. Connect Shopify to Claude and ask it to list paid orders older than 3 days that have not shipped and chart average time to ship per week. Clear the backlog and fix the bottleneck.
playbooks.ask: List every paid order older than 3 days that hasn't shipped, with its age, value and products. Also chart the average time from order to shipment per week for the last 12 weeks.
playbooks.then: Clear the backlog. If the average is rising, find the bottleneck before the complaints start.
steps: Connect Shopify read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if you use one, or upload an unfulfilled orders export.
Run the prompt to list paid orders older than 3 days that have not shipped and chart weekly ship times.
Exclude pre-orders and made-to-order items, which are meant to ship later.
Clear the backlog, and find the bottleneck if average time to ship is rising.
Ask Claude to re-run the check every day.
playbooks.example: 23 orders were more than 5 days old and still not shipped.
playbooks.check: Pre-orders and made-to-order items should be excluded.

faq.q: How do I find unshipped orders in Shopify?
faq.a: Filter orders by paid and unfulfilled, then sort by date. The prompt does this and adds age, value and products so you can act fast.

faq.q: How long is too long to ship an order?
faq.a: It depends on what you promise at checkout. Use your own shipping promise as the line, and act on anything older. Shoppers judge you against the date you showed them.

faq.q: Can other assistants run this?
faq.a: Yes. The prompt works with ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can read your Shopify orders, through a connection or an export. The order data is what matters.

faq.q: Why should I track average ship time?
faq.a: A rising average warns you before complaints and chargebacks arrive. It points to a bottleneck in stock, packing or the carrier. Weekly tracking makes the trend easy to see.

playbooks.title: Bestseller missing from your ads
playbooks.seo_title: Bestsellers missing from your ads? Find them with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Match your top Shopify products by revenue to active Meta ads and spend, and flag top sellers with no ads and slow sellers soaking up budget.
playbooks.hook: Your #3 bestseller isn't in a single live ad.
playbooks.answer: Ad spend drifts away from top sellers when creative is planned around launches or old winners. Connect Shopify and Meta Ads to Claude and ask it to match your top ten products by 60-day revenue to active ads and spend. Brief new ads for uncovered bestsellers, and question spend on products that don't sell.
playbooks.ask: List my top 10 products by revenue over the last 60 days. For each, how many active Meta ads feature it, and how much was spent on those ads? Flag top sellers with no ads, and products getting lots of spend that don't sell.
playbooks.then: Brief new ads for the top sellers with no coverage.
steps: Connect Shopify and Meta Ads to Claude read-only, through a connector or MCP server if available, or upload a Shopify sales-by-product report and a Meta ads export.
Run the prompt so Claude maps each top product to its active ads and spend.
Check whether a top seller sells mainly as an add-on after ads for other products.
Brief new ads for top sellers with no coverage, and review heavy spend on slow sellers.
Re-run monthly.
playbooks.example: The #3 bestseller had zero live ads. A slow seller had 30% of spend.
playbooks.check: A product may sell well because it's what people buy after an ad for something else.

faq.q: Why would a bestseller have no ads?
faq.a: Ad plans often follow launches or past winners, not current sales. A product can climb the sales chart through word of mouth or email while the ad account never catches up.

faq.q: Could a product sell well because of ads for something else?
faq.a: Yes. Some products are what people add after clicking an ad for another item. Check how often the bestseller is bought alongside advertised products before you move spend.

faq.q: Can I run this with ChatGPT, Grok or Muse?
faq.a: Yes. Any of them can use this prompt if it can read your Shopify sales and Meta ads data, either through a connection or from exported reports you upload.

faq.q: How much spend should go to bestsellers?
faq.a: There is no fixed share. Start by giving each top seller at least some ad coverage, then let the results guide how budget moves between products over the following weeks.

playbooks.title: Junk traffic is skewing your numbers
playbooks.seo_title: Bot traffic skewing your conversion rate? Check with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Find bot and junk sessions in GA4 and fake checkouts in Shopify, then see your real conversion and checkout completion rates without them.
playbooks.hook: Before you panic about conversion rate, check how much of your traffic is bots.
playbooks.answer: Junk traffic, like bots, zero-engagement sessions and checkouts with throwaway emails, makes conversion rate look worse than it is. Connect Google Analytics and Shopify to Claude and ask it to find these signs over 60 days and estimate real conversion and checkout completion without them. Filter junk out of reports before deciding anything.
playbooks.ask: Look for signs of bot or junk traffic in the last 60 days: sessions with zero engagement time, spikes from a single city or source, and Shopify checkouts started with throwaway email addresses. Estimate how much it changes my conversion rate and checkout-completion rate once it's removed.
playbooks.then: Filter junk out of your reports before making any decision from them.
steps: Connect Google Analytics and Shopify to Claude read-only, through a connector or MCP server if available, or upload a GA4 sessions export and a Shopify abandoned checkouts report.
Run the prompt so Claude flags zero-engagement sessions, single-source spikes and checkouts with throwaway emails.
Ask Claude to recompute conversion and checkout completion rates with the junk removed.
Set up filters or segments in your reports so junk stays out of future decisions.
Run this weekly, and always before any other conversion playbook.
playbooks.example: Checkout starts tripled overnight, all from throwaway emails. Real completion hadn't moved.
playbooks.check: This is the check. Run it before any conversion playbook.

faq.q: How can I tell bot traffic from real visitors?
faq.a: Bots tend to show zero engagement time, sudden spikes from one city or source, and checkouts with throwaway email addresses. Real shoppers browse, view products and come from a mix of sources.

faq.q: Why run this before other conversion checks?
faq.a: Junk traffic changes the numbers every other check relies on. If bots inflate sessions, conversion rate looks like it fell when real sales did not move. Clean the data first, then diagnose.

faq.q: Will this work in ChatGPT, Grok or Muse?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the assistant can see your Google Analytics and Shopify data. Connect them, or export your sessions and checkout reports and upload the files with the same prompt.

faq.q: Does junk traffic cost me money?
faq.a: It can, if it comes from paid sources or leads you to change things that were working. Often the bigger cost is a bad decision made from skewed numbers, like cutting a channel that was fine.

playbooks.title: A competitor just started a sale
playbooks.seo_title: Competitor launched a sale? Spot it early with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Check your competitors' new Meta ads and websites for fresh sales, discounts, shipping offers and price cuts, summarized in one daily read.
playbooks.hook: Know the morning your closest rival launches a sale, not a week later.
playbooks.answer: Competitor sales often start quietly with a batch of new ads and lower prices. Give Claude web browsing, list your competitors, and ask it to check the Meta Ad Library for ads started in the last seven days and their sites for sale banners or price cuts. Then decide whether to match, counter or hold.
playbooks.ask: For each of these competitors [names], check the Meta Ad Library for ads started in the last 7 days and their websites for sale banners or lowered prices. Summarize what changed: new offers, discounts, free-shipping thresholds and prices on products like mine.
playbooks.then: Decide whether to match, counter with a different offer, or hold.
steps: Give Claude web browsing, or open the Meta Ad Library and your competitors' sites yourself and paste what you find. No login is needed.
Run the prompt with the names of your closest competitors.
Review the summary of new offers, discounts, shipping thresholds and price changes on products like yours.
Watch your own conversion rate while their sale runs before reacting. A sale alone is not a threat.
Decide whether to match, counter with a different offer, or hold.
Schedule the check to run daily.
playbooks.example: A rival launched 30% off with 9 new ads and lower prices on 14 products.
playbooks.check: A sale isn't a threat on its own. Watch whether your own conversion dips while it runs.

faq.q: Should I match a competitor's sale?
faq.a: Not by default. First watch whether your own conversion rate dips while their sale runs. If it holds, you may not need to react. If it drops, a different offer can work as well as matching.

faq.q: Which competitors should I track?
faq.a: Your closest rivals: the stores selling similar products at similar prices to the same shoppers. A short list of three to five keeps a daily check quick and focused.

faq.q: Can ChatGPT run this daily check?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can browse the web, including ChatGPT, Grok and Muse, can run the same prompt. Some can also schedule it, or you can paste it in each morning yourself.

faq.q: Is the Meta Ad Library free to use?
faq.a: Yes. It is public and shows the active ads for any page, along with when each ad started. No ad account or login is needed to read it.

playbooks.title: One funnel step suddenly dropped
playbooks.seo_title: Conversion rate dropped everywhere? Find why with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Track your funnel week by week by channel and device, find the step that fell everywhere at once, and pin down the day it changed.
playbooks.hook: If conversion drops on every channel at once, the problem is your site, not your ads.
playbooks.answer: When conversion falls on every channel at once, a site change is the usual cause: a theme update, a new app or a checkout edit. Connect Google Analytics and Shopify to Claude, ask for eight weeks of funnel steps by channel and device, and find the first day a step fell. Then check what changed that day.
playbooks.ask: Show the funnel for the last 8 weeks, week by week: sessions, product views, add to cart, checkout started, purchase. Split it by channel and by device. Find any step that fell more than 20% across every channel at the same time, and compare with the same weeks last year. Tell me the first day it changed.
playbooks.then: Look at what changed on the site that day: a theme update, a new app, a checkout change.
steps: Connect Google Analytics and Shopify to Claude read-only, through a connector or MCP server if available, or upload a GA4 funnel export and a Shopify orders report.
Run the prompt so Claude builds the weekly funnel by channel and device and compares it with last year.
Rule out bot traffic with the junk-traffic playbook, and rule out normal seasonal dips.
List every site change made on the day the step fell: theme updates, new apps, checkout settings.
Undo or fix that change, then watch the funnel step for the next week.
Re-run weekly so a drop is caught within days.
playbooks.example: Add-to-cart to checkout fell 30% on every channel from the same day an app was installed.
playbooks.check: Rule out bot traffic first (see the junk-traffic playbook) and seasonality (compare with last year).

faq.q: How do I know the problem is my site and not my ads?
faq.a: Check whether the drop shows on every channel at the same time. An ads problem usually hits one channel. A drop across paid, email and organic together points to something on the site itself.

faq.q: What counts as a big enough drop?
faq.a: The playbook flags any step that fell more than 20% across every channel at once. Treat that as a starting threshold, not a rule, and adjust it to how much your numbers normally move week to week.

faq.q: Can I use a different assistant than Claude?
faq.a: Yes. ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can read your Google Analytics and Shopify data will work with the same prompt, whether connected live or given exported reports.

faq.q: What are the most common causes?
faq.a: A theme update, a newly installed app, a change to checkout or shipping settings, or a broken script. Matching the first day of the drop to your list of recent changes usually finds the cause.

playbooks.title: Expired promos still in live ads
playbooks.seo_title: Expired sale ads still running? Find them with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Scan every active Meta ad for dates, deadlines and holiday sales that have already passed, and see how long each one has kept running.
playbooks.hook: An ad that says 'ends Sunday' three weeks later tells shoppers not to trust you.
playbooks.answer: Expired promo ads keep running when a sale ends but nobody turns off the ads tied to it. Give Claude web browsing and ask it to read every active ad in the Meta Ad Library, flag any date, deadline, holiday or sale that has passed, and note run time. Turn those ads off or swap in evergreen versions.
playbooks.ask: Look at every active ad for [brand] in the Meta Ad Library. Find any ad that mentions a date, a deadline, a holiday or a sale that has already passed. List them with how long each has been running.
playbooks.then: Turn them off or swap in an evergreen version.
steps: Give Claude web browsing, or open the Meta Ad Library yourself and paste in your active ads. No login is needed.
Run the prompt for your brand so Claude flags every ad that mentions a passed date, deadline, holiday or sale.
Check the start date and run time Claude lists for each flagged ad, and confirm the sale was not extended.
Turn off each expired ad, or replace it with an evergreen version of the same creative.
Re-run the check weekly and right after every sale or holiday ends.
playbooks.example: Halloween ads still running in mid-November.
playbooks.check: None. Dates in ads either have passed or they haven't.

faq.q: Why do expired promo ads matter if they still get clicks?
faq.a: They promise something the store no longer offers. Shoppers who click a sale that ended often leave, and some stop trusting your future offers. You also keep paying for clicks that are unlikely to convert.

faq.q: Is there an innocent explanation for an ad with an old date?
faq.a: Rarely. A date in an ad has either passed or it hasn't. The one thing to check is whether the sale was extended. If it was, update the ad copy so the date matches.

faq.q: Can ChatGPT or Grok do this check too?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant with web browsing, such as ChatGPT, Grok or Muse, can read the Meta Ad Library with the same prompt. Without browsing, copy your active ads in as text and ask the same question.

faq.q: How do I stop this from happening again?
faq.a: Add a step to your sale checklist: when a sale ends, pause every ad that names it. A weekly run of this playbook catches anything that slips through the checklist.

playbooks.title: Your top ad page is slow on phones
playbooks.seo_title: Landing page slow on mobile? Find the fixes with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Run PageSpeed Insights on the pages your ads link to, see what slows them down on phones, and get the fixes ranked by time saved.
playbooks.hook: Most of your ad clicks are on phones. How long does your page take to load there?
playbooks.answer: Ad landing pages are often slow on phones because of oversized images and apps that load scripts on every page. Give Claude web browsing and ask it to run PageSpeed Insights on mobile for each ad landing page, then rank fixes by time saved. Fix the top two first, and run each test three times.
playbooks.ask: Run Google PageSpeed Insights on mobile for these pages: [the pages your ads link to]. For each, give the load time, the biggest problems, and which apps or scripts add the most weight. Rank the fixes by how much time they'd save.
playbooks.then: Fix the top two (usually oversized images and unused apps).
steps: Give Claude web browsing, or run PageSpeed Insights yourself and paste the mobile results into the chat. No login is needed.
List the pages your ads link to and run the prompt on each one.
Run each test three times and use the typical result, since single runs vary.
Fix the top two items, usually oversized images and unused apps, then retest.
Re-run monthly and after installing any new app or theme update.
playbooks.example: The top ad page took 6.1 seconds on phones. Two apps added 1.8 seconds.
playbooks.check: Run it three times. Single runs vary.

faq.q: What slows a store page down on phones?
faq.a: The common causes are oversized images, apps that load scripts on every page, and heavy fonts or video. PageSpeed Insights lists which files add the most weight, so you can see what to fix first.

faq.q: Why are my PageSpeed results different every time?
faq.a: Single runs vary with network and server conditions. Run each page three times and use the typical result. Compare before and after a fix the same way, so you know the fix really helped.

faq.q: Can I do this with ChatGPT or another assistant?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can browse, including ChatGPT, Grok and Muse, can run PageSpeed Insights with this prompt. If it cannot browse, paste in the report and ask it to rank the fixes.

faq.q: Which pages should I test first?
faq.a: The pages your ads link to, starting with the one that gets the most paid clicks. Most ad clicks come from phones, so always test the mobile version rather than desktop.

playbooks.title: Checkout friction on phones
playbooks.seo_title: Mobile checkout losing sales? Test it with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Walk from your top ad's landing page to checkout on a phone-sized browser and list every point of friction, from forced accounts to surprise shipping.
playbooks.hook: Try to buy from your own store on your phone. Time it.
playbooks.answer: Phone checkouts lose sales when express pay is missing, an account is forced, the size picker breaks or shipping costs appear late. Give Claude web browsing and ask it to walk from your top ad's landing page to checkout on a phone-sized browser, without buying, listing every friction point. Fix anything that adds steps or hides costs.
playbooks.ask: On a phone-sized browser, go from my top ad's landing page to the checkout, without buying. Note every step: is Apple Pay or Shop Pay offered, is an account forced, does the size picker work, do reviews load, is shipping cost a surprise, does the discount field work. List every point of friction.
playbooks.then: Fix anything that forces extra steps or hides costs until the end.
steps: Give Claude web browsing in a fresh, logged-out session, or do the walk-through on your own phone and describe each screen.
Run the prompt from your top ad's landing page so Claude records every step to checkout, without buying.
Repeat in a fresh browser to confirm problems are not caused by a saved login or cart.
Fix anything that forces extra steps or hides costs, such as missing express pay or a required account.
Re-run monthly and after any change to your theme, apps or checkout settings.
playbooks.example: No express pay on phones, and an account was required to check out.
playbooks.check: Test with a fresh browser. Logged-in sessions hide problems.

faq.q: What are the most common mobile checkout problems?
faq.a: Missing express pay like Apple Pay or Shop Pay, a forced account, a size picker that does not work, reviews that fail to load, a broken discount field, and shipping costs that only appear at the end.

faq.q: Why test in a fresh browser?
faq.a: A logged-in session fills in your details and hides problems a new shopper would hit. A fresh, private browser shows the checkout the way a first-time visitor from an ad sees it.

faq.q: Does this work with assistants other than Claude?
faq.a: Yes. ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can browse a site at phone size can follow the same prompt. You can also walk the checkout yourself and paste your notes in.

faq.q: Will Claude place an order?
faq.a: No. The prompt says to stop before buying. It only goes far enough to see each checkout step and what it asks the shopper for, so nothing is charged or shipped.

playbooks.title: Your offer next to your competitors'
playbooks.seo_title: Is your offer weaker than competitors'? Check with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Put your prices, free-shipping threshold, returns, guarantee and payment options next to your competitors' and see where you're weaker or stronger.
playbooks.hook: Their free-shipping bar is $50. Yours is $75. Shoppers notice.
playbooks.answer: Shoppers compare stores on more than price: free-shipping threshold, return window, guarantee, payment options and the current offer. Give Claude web browsing, name your competitors, and ask it to put these side by side with yours. Close the gaps that are cheap to fix, and make your stronger points easier to see.
playbooks.ask: For my store and these competitors [names], put side by side: price on comparable products, free-shipping threshold, return window, guarantee, payment options and the current offer. Show where I'm weaker and where I'm stronger.
playbooks.then: Fix the gaps that are cheap to close. Lean into the ones where you're stronger.
steps: Give Claude web browsing, or paste your competitors' shipping, returns and pricing pages into the chat. No login is needed.
Run the prompt with your store and the competitors you most often lose sales to.
Check that any higher price is explained on your page. Being pricier is fine if shoppers can see why.
Close the gaps that are cheap to fix, such as the return window or shipping threshold.
Make your strengths more visible on product and cart pages.
Re-run monthly.
playbooks.example: Rivals gave 60-day returns against 30, and free shipping at $50 against $75.
playbooks.check: Being pricier is fine if your page explains why. Check that it does.

faq.q: What should I compare besides price?
faq.a: Free-shipping threshold, return window, guarantee, payment options like express pay or pay later, and the current offer. Shoppers often decide on these when prices are close.

faq.q: Is it bad to be more expensive than competitors?
faq.a: Not if your page explains why. Better materials, a longer guarantee or faster shipping can justify a higher price. The check is whether a shopper can actually see the reason on the page.

faq.q: Can I use ChatGPT, Grok or Muse instead?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can browse public store pages can build the same comparison from this prompt. If it cannot browse, paste each store's policy and product pages in.

faq.q: Which gaps should I fix first?
faq.a: The cheap ones. Extending a return window or lowering a shipping threshold often costs less than a discount, and both are easy to test and roll back.

playbooks.title: Ads sent to the homepage
playbooks.seo_title: Product ads landing on your homepage? Fix it with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: See which Meta ads send product clicks to your homepage, compare conversion rate by landing page in GA4, and repoint the ones losing sales.
playbooks.hook: Product ads that land on your homepage usually convert at half the rate.
playbooks.answer: Product ads that land on the homepage make shoppers hunt for what they just saw, so many leave. Connect Meta Ads and Google Analytics to Claude, ask it to group active ads by landing URL and compare ad-traffic conversion rate per page. Point single-product ads at that product page or an offer page.
playbooks.ask: List every active Meta ad and the URL it sends people to. Group by landing page. Using Google Analytics, show the conversion rate of ad traffic on each landing page. Flag ads that send people to the homepage or a general collection while showing one product.
playbooks.then: Point product ads at the product page, or a page built for that offer.
steps: Connect Meta Ads and Google Analytics to Claude read-only, through a connector or MCP server if you have one, or upload an ads export and a GA4 landing page report.
Run the prompt so Claude groups every active ad by landing page and shows ad-traffic conversion rate for each.
Set aside brand ads that show no single product. Those can reasonably go to the homepage.
Repoint each product ad to its product page, or to a page built for that offer.
Re-run monthly and compare conversion rate on the new landing pages.
playbooks.example: 8 ads went to the homepage, which converted at half the rate of product pages.
playbooks.check: Brand ads with no single product can reasonably go to the homepage.

faq.q: Is sending ads to the homepage always wrong?
faq.a: No. Brand or awareness ads that show no single product can go to the homepage. The problem is ads that show one product and then make the shopper search for it after the click.

faq.q: Where do I find which page each ad links to?
faq.a: In Meta Ads Manager, each ad lists its destination URL. An export of active ads with their URLs works well. Claude can then match those URLs to landing pages in Google Analytics.

faq.q: Does this work with ChatGPT or other assistants?
faq.a: It does. The prompt works with ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can read your Meta Ads and Google Analytics data, through a live connection or exported reports.

faq.q: What should a product ad link to?
faq.a: The product page for the item in the ad, or a landing page built for that exact offer. The shopper should see the same product and price they saw in the ad, with nothing to search for.

playbooks.title: Back-in-stock demand left waiting
playbooks.seo_title: Back-in-stock emails not sending? Check with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Match Klaviyo back-in-stock requests to products that are in stock again in Shopify, and see who is still waiting for an email.
playbooks.hook: 210 people asked to hear when it's back. It's back. Nobody told them.
playbooks.answer: Back-in-stock requests go unanswered when the flow is off, in draft, or not tied to restocked items. Connect Klaviyo and Shopify to Claude and ask it to match every request to products now in stock, count waiting shoppers per product, and confirm whether they were emailed. Send the emails now and make the flow live.
playbooks.ask: List every back-in-stock request in Klaviyo for products that are now in stock in Shopify. How many people are waiting per product, and has anyone been emailed?
playbooks.then: Send the back-in-stock emails now and make sure the flow is live.
steps: Connect Klaviyo and Shopify to Claude read-only, through a connector or MCP server if available, or upload a back-in-stock request export and a Shopify inventory report.
Run the prompt so Claude lists waiting shoppers for each product that is now in stock.
Confirm in Klaviyo whether each group was emailed. There is no gray area here.
Send the back-in-stock emails now, and check the flow is live and triggered by inventory changes.
Re-run weekly, and after every restock.
playbooks.example: 210 people waited on a size that had been back for a week.
playbooks.check: None. Either they were emailed or they weren't.

faq.q: Why didn't my back-in-stock flow send?
