faq.a: Common causes are a flow left in draft or turned off, a trigger not linked to inventory updates, or a variant restocked under a new listing. Checking requests against live stock shows which one applies.

faq.q: How fast should I email after a restock?
faq.a: As soon as stock is live. People who asked to be told are among your warmest shoppers, and the item can sell out again before they hear about it.

faq.q: Can I use ChatGPT or Grok for this?
faq.a: Yes. The prompt works with any assistant that can read your Klaviyo requests and Shopify inventory, through a connection or exported files. ChatGPT, Grok and Muse all work this way.

faq.q: What if I have more requests than stock?
faq.a: Email the people who asked first, or send in batches as stock allows. Telling everyone at once can lead to disappointed shoppers or oversold orders if inventory is tight.

playbooks.title: Missing or one-email flows
playbooks.seo_title: Missing Klaviyo flows? Find the gaps with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: List your live Klaviyo flows and email counts, find missing or one-email flows, and rank the gaps by how many people would enter each week.
playbooks.hook: A one-email abandoned-cart flow leaves money on the table every single day.
playbooks.answer: Flow gaps are usually a missing core flow, one still in draft, or a flow with only one email. Connect Klaviyo to Claude and ask it to list live flows with email counts, check for welcome, abandoned checkout, abandoned cart, browse abandonment, post-purchase and win-back, and rank gaps by weekly entries. Build the biggest gap first.
playbooks.ask: List my live flows and how many emails each one sends. Do I have a welcome series, abandoned checkout, abandoned cart, browse abandonment, post-purchase and win-back? Which are missing, in draft, or only one email long? Rank the gaps by how many people would enter each flow per week.
playbooks.then: Build the biggest missing flow first.
steps: Connect Klaviyo to Claude read-only, through a connector or MCP server if available, or upload an export of your flows with status and message counts.
Run the prompt so Claude lists each flow, its status and how many emails it sends.
Have Claude estimate how many people would enter each missing flow per week. A gap with very few entries can wait.
Build the biggest missing flow first, or extend a one-email flow into a short series.
Re-run quarterly and after any account cleanup.
playbooks.example: No browse-abandon flow, a one-email cart flow, and the post-purchase flow still a draft.
playbooks.check: Count the people who'd enter each flow before building. A gap with 10 people a week can wait.

faq.q: Which email flows should every store have?
faq.a: The usual core set is a welcome series, abandoned checkout, abandoned cart, browse abandonment, post-purchase and win-back. Which ones matter most depends on how many people would enter each one.

faq.q: Is a one-email abandoned cart flow enough?
faq.a: Usually not. A short series gives shoppers more than one reminder and room to answer common questions. Start by adding one or two follow-ups and compare results with the single email.

faq.q: Does this prompt work outside Claude?
faq.a: Yes. ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can read your Klaviyo flows, live or from an export, can run the same check and rank the gaps the same way.

faq.q: Which flow should I build first?
faq.a: The one the most people would enter each week. Volume decides the value, so rank gaps by weekly entries before building anything, and leave tiny gaps for later.

playbooks.title: Creator code leaked to coupon sites
playbooks.seo_title: Creator code leaked to coupon sites? Check with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Search coupon sites for your brand's discount codes, see how much of each creator code's use started after it leaked, and replace leaked codes.
playbooks.hook: Search your brand name plus 'discount code'. That's where your margin goes.
playbooks.answer: Creator and influencer codes often end up on coupon sites, so shoppers who were already buying use them and you pay the discount and commission. Connect web search and Shopify to Claude, ask it to list codes shown on coupon sites and chart each one's monthly orders. Retire leaked codes and give creators unique or capped codes.
playbooks.ask: Search the web for '[brand] discount code' and '[brand] promo code'. List every code shown on coupon sites. Then in Shopify, show orders per month for each of those codes and how much of each creator code's use started after it appeared on coupon sites.
playbooks.then: Retire leaked codes and give creators unique, single-use or capped codes.
steps: Give Claude web search and read-only Shopify access, through a connector or MCP server if available, or upload a discount order export.
Run the prompt to list your codes found on coupon sites and chart their monthly orders.
Compare any rise with when the creator posted; more posts can explain more use.
Retire leaked codes and give creators unique, single-use or capped codes.
Re-run the search monthly.
playbooks.example: CREATOR20 is listed on 4 coupon sites and now drives 30% of that code's orders.
playbooks.check: A rise can also be the creator posting more. Compare with when their posts went out.

faq.q: How do I know if my discount code leaked?
faq.a: Search your brand name plus 'discount code' or 'promo code'. If a creator code shows up on coupon sites and its use jumps after that, it leaked.

faq.q: Why is a leaked code a problem?
faq.a: Shoppers who would have paid full price use it at checkout. You lose margin and may pay creator commission on sales the creator did not drive.

faq.q: Can I run this in another assistant?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant with web search and your Shopify discount data, connected or uploaded, can run the prompt. ChatGPT, Grok and Muse all work this way.

faq.q: What code setup prevents leaks?
faq.a: Use unique codes per creator, single-use codes, or codes with a usage cap. Track each one separately so a leak shows up fast. Capped codes also limit the damage if one does leak.

playbooks.title: Codes stacking on top of a promo
playbooks.seo_title: Discount codes stacking on promos? Check with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Find Shopify orders where a discount code stacked on an automatic discount or bundle, see the extra discount cost, and decide what to turn off.
playbooks.hook: Your 'buy 2 get 1' might be getting a second discount on top.
playbooks.answer: Codes can stack on top of an automatic discount or bundle offer when Shopify's combination settings allow it, giving away margin twice. Connect Shopify to Claude and ask it to find 90 days of orders with a code on top of a promo, the extra discount cost, and which codes stack most. Then turn off stacking for those codes.
playbooks.ask: Find orders in the last 90 days that used a discount code on top of an automatic discount or bundle offer. How many orders, and how much extra discount did that cost? Which codes stack most often?
playbooks.then: Turn off stacking for those codes, on a set date and outside a big sale, then compare.
steps: Connect Shopify read-only, through a Claude connector or MCP server if available, or upload a 90-day order export with discount columns.
Run the prompt to find orders where a code stacked on an automatic discount or bundle.
Ask which combinations were meant to be allowed, such as staff codes.
Turn off stacking for the unplanned codes on a set date, outside a big sale, then compare results.
Re-run the check monthly.
playbooks.example: A returning-customer code stacked on the bundle deal. About $900 a month in extra discount.
playbooks.check: Some stacking is planned (for example staff codes). Ask which combinations were meant to be allowed.

faq.q: Can Shopify discount codes stack with automatic discounts?
faq.a: Yes, if the discount's combination settings allow it. Each code and automatic discount has its own settings, so one loose setting can let a code stack on every promo.

faq.q: How much does stacking cost?
faq.a: It depends on your codes and order volume. The prompt adds up the extra discount from stacked orders, for example a monthly total, so you see your own number.

faq.q: Will this work with ChatGPT?
faq.a: Yes. Upload your Shopify order export or connect your store to any assistant that can read it, and the same prompt applies. ChatGPT, Grok and Muse can all work through it.

faq.q: Should I turn off stacking during a sale?
faq.a: Better not. Change it on a quiet date so you can compare before and after without a big sale muddying the numbers. A clean test date gives you a fair read on what stacking costs.

playbooks.title: Count the Amazon halo before cutting Meta
playbooks.seo_title: Check Amazon sales before you cut Meta ads
playbooks.meta_description: Find weeks when Meta spend dropped, see what happened to Amazon and Shopify sales after, and count that before cutting ads.
playbooks.hook: Meta ads can look unprofitable while quietly driving your Amazon sales.
playbooks.answer: Meta ads can look unprofitable on site sales while also driving Amazon sales. Connect Meta Ads, Shopify and Amazon Seller Central, ask Claude to find weeks when Meta spend was cut or paused, what happened to Amazon and Shopify sales after, and your Amazon share of sales. If Amazon dropped when Meta paused, count that before cutting.
playbooks.ask: Over the last 12 months, find any week where Meta spend was cut sharply or paused. What happened to Amazon sales and Shopify sales in the weeks after? What share of my total sales is on Amazon?
playbooks.then: If Amazon sales dropped when Meta paused, count that before cutting.
steps: Connect Meta Ads, Shopify and Amazon Seller Central read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export weekly spend and sales reports and upload them.
Ask the playbook prompt to find past Meta cuts or pauses and compare Amazon and Shopify sales in the weeks after.
Check what else changed then, such as prices, Amazon ads or stock. Treat the result as a warning, not proof.
If you still cut, do it in steps with a review date and watch Amazon sales weekly.
Re-run this before any big cut, and compare with the same weeks last year.
playbooks.example: Meta looked weak on site sales, but 35% of sales were on Amazon.
playbooks.check: Other things change at the same time (prices, Amazon ads). Treat this as a warning, not proof.

faq.q: What is the Amazon halo effect?
faq.a: It is when ads seen on Meta lead people to buy on Amazon instead of your site. Meta cannot track those sales, so its reports undercount what the ads do.

faq.q: How can I tell if Meta drives my Amazon sales?
faq.a: Look at past weeks when Meta spend dropped sharply. If Amazon sales fell soon after and nothing else changed, that is a sign. A planned holdout by region gives a clearer read.

faq.q: Is this proof that Meta works?
faq.a: No. Other things often change at the same time, like prices, Amazon ads or stock levels. Use it as a warning to test carefully, not as proof to keep spending.

faq.q: Will another assistant handle this prompt?
faq.a: Yes. ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can read your ad spend and sales from both channels can run it, connected or from weekly exports.

playbooks.title: Map which ad angles you've never tried
playbooks.seo_title: Find the ad angles you have never tried
playbooks.meta_description: Tag your ads by angle, audience and format, compare with your competitors, and fill the most promising empty spots with new ads.
playbooks.hook: Most brands run the same three ad ideas in different colours.
playbooks.answer: Many stores run the same few ad ideas in different colors. Connect Meta Ads, open the Meta Ad Library, and ask Claude to tag your ads by angle, audience and format, show the grid with empty cells, and do the same for your competitors. Fill the most promising empty cells with new ads and compare on cost per sale.
playbooks.ask: Tag every active and recent ad I've run by angle (problem, benefit, social proof, comparison, offer, founder story), by audience it speaks to, and by format (static, video, UGC, carousel). Show it as a grid and highlight the empty cells. Do the same for my 3 closest competitors.
playbooks.then: Fill the most promising empty cells with new ads. Let Meta sort them.
steps: Connect Meta Ads read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export your ad list, and give Claude the Meta Ad Library through browsing.
Ask the playbook prompt to tag ads by angle, audience and format and show empty cells for you and your competitors.
Check which empty cells competitors fill with long-running ads. Empty does not mean good.
Launch new ads in the most promising empty cells on a capped test budget.
Compare new ads on cost per sale against current ones, and re-run the grid monthly.
playbooks.example: 5 ads in 6 months, all the same angle. Competitors had launched 25 that month.
playbooks.check: Empty doesn't mean good. Start with cells where competitors have long-running ads.

faq.q: What is an ad angle?
faq.a: It is the main idea an ad uses to persuade, such as a problem, a benefit, social proof, a comparison, an offer or a founder story. Two ads with different colors but the same idea share one angle.

faq.q: Why look at competitors' long-running ads?
faq.a: Advertisers tend to keep ads that pay for themselves. A competitor ad that has run for months suggests that angle may work in your category. It is a hint, not proof.

faq.q: How many new ads should I launch?
faq.a: Start with a few cells, one or two ads each, so each gets enough budget to read. Let cost per sale decide which angles to expand.

faq.q: Does this prompt work outside Claude?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can read your ads and the public Ad Library, such as ChatGPT, Grok or Muse, can run it from a connection, links or an exported ad list.

playbooks.title: Find regions buying below their share
playbooks.seo_title: Find regions that buy below their population share
playbooks.meta_description: Compare each state's share of your orders with its share of population, check Meta delivery there, and test regional ads on a cap.
playbooks.hook: Some big states may buy far less from you than their population says they should.
playbooks.answer: Some large states or regions may buy far less from you than their population suggests. Connect Shopify and Meta Ads, ask Claude to compare each region's share of orders with its share of population, and check whether your ads reach those regions. Fix delivery gaps first, then test a regional angle on a capped budget.
playbooks.ask: Break down my Shopify orders for the last 12 months by state (or region). Compare each one's share of orders with its share of the population. Then check Meta delivery by region. Which large regions buy well below their share, and are my ads even reaching them?
playbooks.then: Fix delivery first. Then test a regional angle on a capped budget.
steps: Connect Shopify and Meta Ads read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export orders by region and ad delivery reports and upload them.
Ask the playbook prompt to compare order share with population share by region and check ad delivery.
Check shipping times and weather first. They explain some gaps and spending will not fix them.
Fix delivery gaps, then test a regional angle on a capped budget with a review date.
Compare orders from that region with last year or with a similar region you left alone, and re-run twice a year.
playbooks.example: Three large states bought well below their population share.
playbooks.check: Shipping time and weather explain some gaps. Check those before spending.

faq.q: Why would a big state buy less than expected?
faq.a: Common reasons are slow or costly shipping, weather or season, local competitors, or ads that rarely reach that region. The data shows the gap. Checking these reasons tells you whether it can be fixed.

faq.q: Where do I get population data?
faq.a: Public census figures by state or region work fine. Claude can look them up with web search or you can supply a table. You only need shares, not exact counts.

faq.q: How do I measure a regional test?
faq.a: Compare orders from the tested region with the same period last year, or with a similar region you did not change. That gives a fair baseline instead of claiming the whole lift.

faq.q: Will this work with other assistants?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can read your orders and ad delivery data, including ChatGPT, Grok or Muse, can run this prompt from a connection or exported files.

playbooks.title: Fill in what AI shopping assistants ask for
playbooks.seo_title: Get your products named by AI shopping assistants
playbooks.meta_description: Ask AI assistants the questions your buyers ask, see which brands and sites they cite, and add the missing facts to product pages.
playbooks.hook: When someone asks ChatGPT for the best product in your category, are you in the answer?
playbooks.answer: When shoppers ask AI assistants for the best product, your brand may not appear. Using a web browser and web search, ask Claude to run several best-product questions, note which brands and sites are cited, and check whether your product pages state use case, size, materials, price and audience. Add missing facts and seek coverage on cited sites.
playbooks.ask: Ask: 'What's the best [product type] for [use case] under [price]?' and 5 similar questions. Which brands are named, and which sites are cited? Then read my top 10 product pages: do they clearly state use case, size, materials, price and who it's for?
playbooks.then: Add those facts to your pages. Get onto the review sites and threads the answers cite.
steps: Give Claude web search and browsing so it can run buyer questions and read your top product pages. No login is needed.
Ask the playbook prompt to run the questions, list named brands and cited sites, and check your pages for key facts.
Check the answers over a few weeks. They change day to day, so one run is not a trend.
Add clear facts to your product pages: use case, size, materials, price and who it is for.
Pursue coverage on the review sites and threads the answers cite, and re-run the same questions monthly.
playbooks.example: The brand was missing from 7 of 10 'best X' answers. 70% of product pages didn't state size or use case.
playbooks.check: Answers change day to day. Track the same questions over a few weeks.

faq.q: How do AI assistants choose which products to recommend?
faq.a: They draw on pages and sources they can read, such as review sites, forums and product pages. Pages that state clear facts are easier to quote. The exact method varies by assistant.

faq.q: What should my product pages say?
faq.a: State the plain facts a buyer asks about: what it is for, size, materials, price and who it suits. Put them in text, not only in images, so assistants and search engines can read them.

faq.q: How do I know if it is working?
faq.a: Track the same set of questions every few weeks and record whether your brand appears. Answers change often, so look at the trend over time, not a single day.

faq.q: Should I test this in ChatGPT too?
faq.a: Yes. Run the same questions in ChatGPT, Grok, Muse and other assistants, since each draws on different sources. The prompt works in any assistant that can browse the web.

playbooks.title: Run ads when a competitor's hero sells out
playbooks.seo_title: Run ads when a competitor's bestseller sells out
playbooks.meta_description: Watch competitor bestseller pages daily, spot when one sells out, and run a capped ad budget aimed at its buyers until it restocks.
playbooks.hook: When your rival's bestseller is out of stock, their customers are looking for you.
playbooks.answer: When a competitor's bestseller is out of stock, its shoppers look elsewhere. Using a web browser and the Meta Ad Library, ask Claude to check those product pages daily, report when one shows sold out and for how long, and whether its ads still run. Run a capped ad budget aimed at those buyers and stop the day it restocks.
playbooks.ask: Check the product pages of these competitor bestsellers every day: [links]. Tell me the day any of them shows sold out, and how long it stays out. Also note whether their ads for it are still running in the Meta Ad Library.
playbooks.then: Run a capped budget of ads aimed at that product's buyers until they restock.
steps: Give Claude the competitor product page links and the Meta Ad Library through web browsing. No login is needed.
Ask the playbook prompt to check the pages daily and report sold-out dates and whether their ads still run.
Check the page really shows sold out for all main sizes, not one variant or region.
Run a small capped ad budget aimed at that product's buyers, with a hard stop on the restock day.
Compare cost per sale with your usual ads, and keep the daily check running.
playbooks.example: A rival's bestseller was sold out for four days. A small conquest budget ran until it came back.
playbooks.check: Cap the budget and stop the day they restock.

faq.q: Is it allowed to advertise when a competitor sells out?
faq.a: Yes, as long as your ads are truthful and do not misuse their trademarks. Target shoppers interested in the product type rather than claiming to be the brand. Check each ad platform's rules.

faq.q: How do I track competitor stock every day?
faq.a: Ask Claude to visit the product pages once a day and note whether each shows sold out. A scheduled run or a simple reminder keeps it going.

faq.q: How much should I spend?
faq.a: Keep it small and capped, and stop the day they restock. The window is short and the extra demand fades once the product is back.

faq.q: Can other assistants run the daily check?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can browse public pages, such as ChatGPT, Grok or Muse, can run this prompt. The data is public, so no login is needed.

playbooks.title: Put money behind your best organic post
playbooks.seo_title: Turn your best organic social posts into ads
playbooks.meta_description: Find your top Instagram and Facebook posts from the last 90 days that were never run as ads, and test them on a capped budget.
playbooks.hook: Your best organic post may have beaten every ad you ran, and it was never boosted.
playbooks.answer: Your best organic post may have beaten your ads without ever being boosted. Using your social accounts and Meta Ads, ask Claude for your top posts from the last 90 days, which were never used as ads, and how their engagement compares. Run the best ones as ads on a capped budget and judge them on cost per sale.
playbooks.ask: List my top 10 Instagram and Facebook posts from the last 90 days by engagement and reach. Which were never used as ads? Compare their engagement rate with my active ads.
playbooks.then: Run the best ones as ads on a capped budget. Compare on cost per sale.
steps: Connect your social accounts and Meta Ads read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export post and ad reports and upload them.
Ask the playbook prompt for your top posts by engagement and reach, and which were never run as ads.
Check that a post's engagement is not mostly from existing fans or a giveaway. Engagement is not sales.
Run the best posts as ads on a capped budget with a stop date.
Compare them with current ads on cost per sale, and re-run the list monthly.
playbooks.example: The top organic post beat every ad on engagement and was never boosted.
playbooks.check: Engagement isn't sales. Judge it on cost per sale once it runs.

faq.q: Is boosting a post the same as running it as an ad?
faq.a: Close, but running the post through Ads Manager gives you more control over audience, budget and tracking. Either way, judge it on cost per sale rather than likes.

faq.q: Why might an organic post do well as an ad?
faq.a: It has already held attention with real people, without paid reach. That makes it a good candidate to test. Paid audiences differ from followers, so the result can change.

faq.q: How much should I spend on the test?
faq.a: Set a cap you are fine losing, and a stop date. For example, a small daily budget for a week or two. Then compare cost per sale with your current ads before spending more.

faq.q: Can I use another AI assistant for this?
faq.a: Yes. ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can read your post and ad performance can run this prompt, either through a connection or from exported reports.

playbooks.title: Turn your best email subject line into an ad
playbooks.seo_title: Turn your best email subject lines into ad hooks
playbooks.meta_description: Find your top email subject lines from the past year, check whether any became ad hooks, and draft new ad hooks from the rest.
playbooks.hook: Your best-performing subject line has probably never been used as an ad hook.
playbooks.answer: Your best email subject lines have already been tested on real customers, yet they may never have appeared in an ad. Connect Klaviyo and Meta Ads, ask Claude for your top campaigns by open or click rate and whether those lines were used as ad hooks. Draft hooks from the unused ones, launch them, and compare on cost per sale.
playbooks.ask: List my 10 email campaigns with the highest open rate in the last 12 months, with their subject lines. Then check my Meta ads: has any of those lines or ideas been used as an ad hook? Draft 3 ad hooks from the unused ones.
playbooks.then: Launch them as new ads and let Meta sort them on cost per sale.
steps: Connect Klaviyo and Meta Ads read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export campaign and ad reports and upload them.
Ask the playbook prompt for your top subject lines and whether each has been used as an ad hook.
Check click rate as well as open rate, since Apple Mail inflates opens.
Launch the drafted hooks as new ads on a capped budget alongside your current ads.
Compare on cost per sale after a fair test period, and re-run the check each quarter.
playbooks.example: A subject line opened at 42% and had never been used in an ad.
playbooks.check: Open rates are inflated by Apple Mail. Prefer click rate if you have it.

faq.q: Why would an email subject line work as an ad?
faq.a: A subject line that many subscribers opened has already shown it catches attention. The same idea can work as the first line of an ad. It is a starting point to test, not a sure win.

faq.q: Are open rates reliable for this?
faq.a: Not fully. Apple Mail privacy features can mark emails as opened when no one read them. Prefer click rate when you have it, and use open rate only to shortlist ideas.

faq.q: How many hooks should I test?
faq.a: Start with a few, such as three, so each gets enough budget to read. Run them alongside your current ads and let results on cost per sale decide which to keep.

faq.q: Can ChatGPT or Grok do this?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant with access to your email and ad data can run this prompt, whether through a connection or from campaign and ad reports you export and upload.

playbooks.title: Read early sales on a new drop and reorder fast
playbooks.seo_title: When to reorder a new product: read early sales with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Compare daily sales on new products with plan, adjusted for stock-outs and discounts, and see which to reorder now and which to stop pushing.
playbooks.hook: Ten days of sales tell you whether to reorder, if you adjust for stock and price.
playbooks.answer: Early sales on a new product can tell you whether to reorder within about ten days, if you adjust for stock-outs and discounts. Connect Shopify to Claude and ask it to compare sales per day with plan for products launched in the last 30 days. Judge on days 4 to 10, then reorder strong sellers.
playbooks.ask: For products launched in the last 30 days, compare sales per day with what I planned. Adjust for days out of stock and any discount. Which are running well above or below plan? Which should I reorder now?
playbooks.then: Reorder the strong ones before they sell out. Stop pushing the weak ones.
steps: Connect Shopify to Claude read-only, through a connector or MCP server if available, or upload daily sales and inventory for recent launches with your sales plan.
Run the prompt so Claude compares sales per day with plan, adjusted for days out of stock and discounts.
Ignore the first three days. Your email list inflates launch-week sales, so read days 4 to 10.
Reorder products running well above plan, and stop pushing those well below it.
Re-run weekly for every new launch.
playbooks.example: After 10 days, a new colour was running at 2.3 times plan.
playbooks.check: Launch-week sales are inflated by your email list. Look at days 4 to 10.

faq.q: Why skip the first few days of a launch?
faq.a: Launch-week sales are inflated by your email list and most loyal buyers. Days 4 to 10 show demand from everyone else, which is closer to what the product will sell over time.

faq.q: How do stock-outs affect the read?
faq.a: A product that sold out for three days looks weaker than it is. Claude divides sales by the days it was actually in stock, so the rate reflects real demand rather than empty shelves.

faq.q: Can ChatGPT or Muse run this?
faq.a: Yes. The prompt works with any assistant that can read your Shopify sales and inventory, including ChatGPT, Grok and Muse, through a connection or an uploaded export.

faq.q: What if I didn't set a sales plan?
faq.a: Compare with a similar past launch over the same days instead. That still shows whether the new product is running ahead of or behind what you would normally expect.

playbooks.title: Answer the top objection no ad addresses
playbooks.seo_title: Find customer objections your ads never answer
playbooks.meta_description: List the top worries in your low-star reviews and comments, check which your live ads answer, and make ads for the gaps.
playbooks.hook: Your top customer objection probably appears in zero of your ads.
playbooks.answer: Your top customer objection may appear in none of your ads. Using public reviews, social comments and the Meta Ad Library, ask Claude to list the top five worries buyers have, then check which ones at least one live ad answers. Make new ads that answer the uncovered objections directly, and compare them with existing ads on cost per sale.
playbooks.ask: From my 1-3 star reviews and the questions in my social comments, list the top 5 objections or worries people have before or after buying. Then check every active ad in the Meta Ad Library for [brand]: which objections does at least one ad answer, and which does none?
playbooks.then: Make ads that answer the uncovered objections directly.
steps: Give Claude your review pages, social comments and Meta Ad Library page through web browsing, or export reviews and comments and upload them.
Ask the playbook prompt to list the top objections and check each live ad for whether it answers them.
Check that an objection is common, not one loud comment, and that you can answer it truthfully.
Launch a few ads that answer the uncovered objections on a capped test budget.
Compare new ads with existing ones on cost per sale, not clicks, and re-run the map monthly.
playbooks.example: The top objection was fit. None of 40 live ads mentioned it.
playbooks.check: Compare new ads on cost per sale, not clicks.

faq.q: Where do I find customer objections?
faq.a: Start with one- to three-star reviews and the questions people ask in your social comments. They show what worried buyers before purchase or let them down after. Support emails help too if you have them.

faq.q: Should ads talk about negatives?
faq.a: Ads should answer the worry, not repeat it. If fit is the top concern, an ad can show how sizing works or what the return policy is. That meets the objection head on without leading with a negative.

faq.q: How should I judge the new ads?
faq.a: Use cost per sale over a fair test period, not clicks or likes. An objection ad may get fewer clicks but more buyers, because it reaches people who were close to buying.

faq.q: Does this need Claude specifically?
faq.a: No. Any assistant that can read your reviews, comments and the public Ad Library, such as ChatGPT, Grok or Muse, can run the same prompt from links or exported files.

playbooks.title: Set your free-shipping threshold from your real orders
playbooks.seo_title: Set your free-shipping threshold from real order data
playbooks.meta_description: Use 90 days of Shopify orders to see where order values cluster and set a free-shipping threshold that nudges more orders up.
playbooks.hook: If most orders are $62 and free shipping starts at $100, almost nobody reaches it.
playbooks.answer: If your free-shipping threshold sits well above your typical order, few shoppers reach it. Connect Shopify, ask Claude for the spread of order values over 90 days and the share of orders just below the threshold, then pick one that nudges those orders up. Change it on a set date and compare order value, shipping cost and margin.
playbooks.ask: Show the spread of my order values for the last 90 days. Where is the free-shipping threshold, and what share of orders sit within $10 below it? Suggest a threshold that would nudge the most orders up without giving free shipping to orders that already qualify.
playbooks.then: Change it on a set date and compare average order value and shipping cost before and after.
steps: Connect Shopify read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export 90 days of orders as a CSV and upload it.
Ask the playbook prompt for the spread of order values and the share of orders sitting just below your current threshold.
Check margin, not just order value. Free shipping costs money, so confirm the new threshold still pays after shipping.
Change the threshold on a set date and note it. Set a review date about 30 days out.
Compare average order value, shipping cost and margin before and after, and re-run the analysis each quarter.
playbooks.example: 38% of orders sat $3 to $9 below the next useful threshold.
playbooks.check: Read the margin, not just order value. Free shipping costs money.

faq.q: What is a good free-shipping threshold?
faq.a: There is no single right number. A useful threshold sits a little above where many of your orders already land, so shoppers can reach it by adding one item. Your own order data shows where that is.

faq.q: Will lowering the threshold lose money?
faq.a: It can. You pay shipping on more orders, and some orders that would have qualified anyway get it for free. That is why you should read margin after shipping, not just average order value, before and after the change.

faq.q: How long should I wait before judging the change?
faq.a: Give it a few weeks of normal trading, outside a big sale. Compare the same metrics for a similar period before the change. Seasonal swings can look like a result, so also compare with the same weeks last year if you can.

faq.q: Does this work with ChatGPT, Grok or Muse?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can read your Shopify orders can run the same prompt. Connect it if the assistant supports that, or export your orders to a CSV file and upload it.

playbooks.title: Turn review language into page copy
playbooks.seo_title: Use customer review language in your product copy
playbooks.meta_description: Find the phrases and worries customers repeat in reviews, check which your product page misses, and add them near the top.
playbooks.hook: Your customers already wrote your best product description. It's in your reviews.
playbooks.answer: Your reviews hold the words customers use to explain why they buy and what worried them first. Using public reviews and a browser, ask Claude to find the most repeated phrases and worries for a product, then check which ones the product page already covers. Add the missing ones near the top of the page and watch add-to-cart rate.
playbooks.ask: Read my product reviews for [product]. Find the phrases customers repeat most when they explain why they love it or what they were worried about before buying. Then check the product page: which of those phrases and worries does it already cover, and which are missing?
playbooks.then: Add the missing phrases to the page, starting near the top. Watch add-to-cart rate.
steps: Give Claude your public review pages and product page URL through web browsing, or export your reviews as a CSV and upload it.
Ask the playbook prompt to find repeated praise and worries, then compare them with the current product page.
Check that a phrase is common across many reviews, not loud in a few. Skip claims you cannot back up.
Update one page at a time on a set date, starting near the top. Note the date.
Compare add-to-cart rate before and after, then repeat for the next product each quarter.
playbooks.example: 'Doesn't irritate my skin' appeared in 200 reviews and on no page.
playbooks.check: Change one page at a time, on a set date, so you can read the effect.

faq.q: Why use review wording instead of writing my own copy?
faq.a: Customers describe the product in the words other shoppers search and think in. Those phrases often name the exact worry a new buyer has. Your own copy may describe features instead.

faq.q: Which reviews should I read?
faq.a: Read both happy and unhappy reviews. Five-star reviews show why people love it. Lower ratings and early questions show what worried them before buying, which is often the gap on your page.

faq.q: Why change only one page at a time?
faq.a: If you change many pages at once, you cannot tell which change moved the number. One page, on a set date, gives you a clean before and after for add-to-cart rate.

faq.q: Can I paste this prompt into ChatGPT?
faq.a: Yes. The prompt works in ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can browse your review and product pages, or read a review export you upload.

playbooks.title: Ask customers who never came back why
playbooks.seo_title: Ask one-time customers why they never came back
playbooks.meta_description: Find first-time buyers who never reordered, returned or complained, and send a short honest survey email to learn what to fix.
playbooks.hook: The customers who never complained and never came back know something you don't.
playbooks.answer: Customers who never complained and never came back often know what to fix. Connect Shopify and Klaviyo, ask Claude to find first-time buyers from 3 to 12 months ago who never reordered, returned or contacted support, and draft a short three-question email with no discount. Send it, read every answer, and use it to decide what to fix.
playbooks.ask: Find first-time customers from 3 to 12 months ago who never ordered again, never returned anything and never contacted support. How many are there? Draft a short, honest 3-question email asking why, with no discount attached.
playbooks.then: Send it. Read every answer. Use it to decide what to fix, not to claim a result.
steps: Connect Shopify and Klaviyo read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export orders, returns and support contacts and upload them.
Ask the playbook prompt to count these quiet customers and draft the short three-question email.
Check that the list excludes people who unsubscribed, returned items or already got a win-back offer.
Send the email to the segment, with no discount attached, and read every reply.
Use the answers to choose what to fix, not to report revenue. Re-run twice a year.
playbooks.example: 1,100 good first-time buyers never came back and never got in touch.
playbooks.check: This guides decisions. Don't report it as revenue.

faq.q: Why not offer a discount in the email?
faq.a: A discount changes why people reply and attracts bargain answers. A plain, honest question gets more useful feedback about what kept them from buying again.

faq.q: What should the three questions ask?
faq.a: Keep them short and open. For example: what you hoped for, whether the product met it, and what would bring you back. Claude drafts a version you can edit.

faq.q: Can I count the replies as revenue?
faq.a: No. This guides decisions about what to fix. If a fix later lifts repeat orders, measure that separately against last year or a held-back group.

faq.q: Can I send this prompt to ChatGPT or Muse?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can read your orders, returns and email list, including ChatGPT, Grok or Muse, can run it, connected or from exported files.

playbooks.title: Check whether deep first discounts buy worse customers
playbooks.seo_title: Check if deep first-order discounts hurt repeat buys
playbooks.meta_description: Group first-time customers by the discount on their first order and compare repeat rate and revenue per customer after six months.
playbooks.hook: Customers won at 30% off may come back far less than those won at 10%.
playbooks.answer: Customers won with a deep first discount may come back less than those won with a small one. Connect Shopify and ask Claude to group first-time customers from the last 18 months by first-order discount, then show repeat rate and revenue per customer after six months. If deep discounts bring weaker customers, test a smaller welcome offer.
playbooks.ask: Group first-time customers from the last 18 months by the discount on their first order: none, up to 10%, 10-20%, over 20%. For each group, show the repeat-purchase rate and revenue per customer after 6 months.
playbooks.then: If deep discounts bring worse customers, test a smaller welcome offer.
steps: Connect Shopify read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export 18 months of orders with discount codes as a CSV and upload it.
Ask the playbook prompt to group first orders by discount depth and compare repeat rate and revenue after six months.
Check whether deep discounts mostly ran in big sales. Compare groups within the same season.
Test a smaller welcome offer on part of new visitors, keeping the current offer for the rest.
Compare repeat rate between the two groups after a few months, and re-run twice a year.
playbooks.example: Customers won at 30% off repeated 40% less than those won at 10% off.
playbooks.check: Deep discounts often run in big sales, which bring different shoppers. Compare within the same season.

faq.q: Do deep discounts always bring worse customers?
faq.a: No. Sometimes they bring in loyal buyers who would not have tried you otherwise. That is why you check your own data instead of assuming. The pattern differs by store and product.

faq.q: Why wait six months to compare?
faq.a: Repeat purchases take time. Six months gives most customers a fair chance to order again. Shorter windows can make every group look similar, which hides the real difference.

faq.q: What if deep discounts only ran during big sales?
faq.a: Then the shoppers differ, not just the discount. Compare groups won in the same season or sale period so you are not mixing holiday buyers with everyday buyers.

faq.q: Can I paste the prompt into ChatGPT or Muse?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can read your Shopify orders and discount codes can use it, whether it connects directly or reads an order export you upload.

playbooks.title: Price the cost of late deliveries
playbooks.seo_title: Measure how late deliveries hurt repeat orders
playbooks.meta_description: Compare second-order rates for first orders delivered on time versus late, and use the gap to weigh the cost of faster shipping.
playbooks.hook: A first order that arrives late may cost you the second one.
playbooks.answer: A first order that arrives late may cost you the second order. Connect Shopify and ask Claude to split first-time orders from the last 12 months into on time and three or more days late, then compare the share of each group that ordered again within 90 days. Use any gap to weigh the cost of faster shipping.
playbooks.ask: For first-time orders in the last 12 months, compare the time from order to delivery. Split them into on time and 3+ days late. What share of each group placed a second order within 90 days?
playbooks.then: If late orders repeat much less, that's the cost to set against faster shipping.
steps: Connect Shopify read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export orders with fulfillment and delivery dates as a CSV and upload it.
Ask the playbook prompt to compare 90-day repeat rates for on-time and late first orders.
Check that late orders are not mostly from one region or product, which would skew the comparison.
Use the gap to price faster shipping or a better carrier, and test it on a set date.
Compare repeat rates before and after the change, and re-run twice a year.
playbooks.example: Late first orders repeated at 14%. On-time ones at 22%.
playbooks.check: Carrier delays are close to random, which makes this a fair comparison. Check that late orders weren't mostly from one region.

faq.q: Why do late first orders matter so much?
faq.a: The first order sets the customer's view of your store. A late delivery can make them less likely to try you again, even if the product was fine.

faq.q: Is this a fair comparison?
faq.a: Mostly, because carrier delays are close to random. Still check that late orders were not mostly from one region, product or sale period, since those can differ in repeat rate for other reasons.

faq.q: Does Shopify track delivery dates?
faq.a: Shopify records fulfillment, and many carriers send delivery status back through tracking. If delivery dates are missing, use the shipping app or carrier export instead.

faq.q: Can I run this in another assistant?
faq.a: Yes. ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can read your order and delivery data can run it, through a connection or from an export file.

playbooks.title: Put your bundle offer on product pages
playbooks.seo_title: Show your bundle offer on product pages
playbooks.meta_description: Compare single-item orders from product pages with other entry points, check where your bundle offer appears, and test it on product pages.
playbooks.hook: Your bundle deal might only show up in places most buyers never see.
playbooks.answer: Your bundle or multi-buy offer may only appear on pages most buyers never visit. Connect Shopify and Google Analytics, ask Claude to compare the single-item order share for orders that started on product pages versus elsewhere, and where the offer appears. If product pages show more single-item orders, add the bundle there and compare before and after.
playbooks.ask: Compare orders that started on a product page with orders that started elsewhere. What share are single-item orders in each? Where does my bundle or multi-buy offer actually appear on the site?
playbooks.then: Show the bundle on product pages, then compare the single-item share before and after.
steps: Connect Shopify and Google Analytics read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export orders and landing page reports and upload them.
Ask the playbook prompt to compare single-item order share by starting page and list where the bundle offer appears.
Check that the comparison does not fall inside a big sale, since promo traffic changes order size.
Add the bundle offer to product pages on a set date, outside a big sale. Note the date.
Compare the single-item share and order value before and after, then re-check if you change the offer.
playbooks.example: 64% of product-page orders were single items, against 45% elsewhere.
playbooks.check: Run the change outside a big sale so promo traffic doesn't skew it.

faq.q: Where should a bundle offer go on a product page?
faq.a: Near the add-to-cart button, where shoppers decide. An offer buried in a collection page or a footer banner reaches few product-page buyers. Check your own pages to see where it shows today.

faq.q: Why compare orders that start on product pages?
faq.a: Many shoppers land straight on a product page from an ad or search. If those orders are mostly single items while others are not, the offer is likely missing where those shoppers decide.

faq.q: How do I know the change worked?
faq.a: Compare the single-item share and average order value for a few weeks before and after the change, outside any big sale. Treat the gap as a guide, not proof, since other things can change at the same time.

faq.q: Can another assistant run this instead of Claude?
faq.a: Yes. ChatGPT, Grok, Muse or any assistant that can read your order and analytics data can use the same prompt, whether it connects to the tools or reads exported reports.

playbooks.title: Use past stock-outs to decide what to restock
playbooks.seo_title: Decide what to restock from past stock-outs, with Claude
playbooks.meta_description: Look back at every stock-out in the last year, see whether sales moved to similar products or vanished, and restock what shoppers won't replace.
playbooks.hook: Every time a product sold out, you ran a free experiment. Read it.
playbooks.answer: Past stock-outs show which products shoppers will replace and which they won't. Connect Shopify to Claude and ask it to find every top-product stock-out of three days or more in the last year, measure how much demand moved to similar items, and rank products by sales lost per day. Restock first where sales vanished.
playbooks.ask: Find every period in the last 12 months where a top product was sold out for 3 days or more. For each, how much of its usual sales moved to similar products, and how much simply disappeared? Rank products by sales lost per day out of stock.
playbooks.then: Restock first the products whose sales vanish when they're gone, not those whose buyers switch.
steps: Connect Shopify to Claude read-only, through a connector or MCP server if available, or upload 12 months of daily sales by product and inventory history.
Run the prompt so Claude finds each stock-out and measures how much demand moved to similar products.
Check that ad spend stayed steady during each stock-out, since a spend change would confuse the read.
Restock first the products whose sales vanish when they are gone.
Re-run before each stock order.
playbooks.example: When one colour sold out, 70% of its sales moved to another. A different product's stock-outs lost almost everything.
playbooks.check: Make sure ad spend didn't change during the stock-out. That would confuse the read.

faq.q: How do I know if shoppers switched to another product?
faq.a: Compare sales of similar products during the stock-out with their usual rate. If they rose by about what the missing product normally sold, buyers switched. If not, those sales were lost.

faq.q: Why does ad spend matter here?
faq.a: If you cut or raised ads during a stock-out, sales of other products move for that reason too. Pick periods where spend stayed steady, or note the change so you can read around it.

faq.q: Can I do this with an assistant other than Claude?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can read your Shopify sales and inventory history, such as ChatGPT, Grok or Muse, can run the prompt on a live connection or an exported file.

faq.q: What if I don't have stock history?
faq.a: Days with zero sales of a normally steady product are a rough stand-in for a stock-out. Shopify inventory reports can also show when stock hit zero for each item.

playbooks.title: Judge ads on sales after returns
playbooks.seo_title: Measure ROAS after returns and refunds
playbooks.meta_description: Work out return on ad spend per category before and after refunds, and find categories that look good until returns come back.
playbooks.hook: A category with great ROAS can lose once you count what comes back.
playbooks.answer: A category with strong return on ad spend can lose money once refunds are counted. Connect Shopify, Meta Ads and Google Ads, ask Claude for revenue, refund rate and ad spend by category over six months, and compare ROAS before and after refunds. Lower spend on high-return categories and fix the reason for returns, often sizing.
playbooks.ask: For each product category, show revenue, refund rate and ad spend for the last 6 months. Work out return on ad spend before and after refunds. Which categories look good before returns and bad after?
playbooks.then: Lower bids or spend on high-return categories. Fix the reason for returns (often sizing).
steps: Connect Shopify, Meta Ads and Google Ads read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export orders, refunds and ad spend and upload them.
Ask the playbook prompt to compare ROAS before and after refunds for each product category.
Use orders at least 45 days old so refunds have time to come in.
Lower bids or spend on high-return categories in steps, and set a review date. Look into the main return reason.
Compare net ROAS after the change with the prior period, and re-run each quarter.
playbooks.example: One category showed 3.1x ROAS, but 34% came back. Net of returns, a 2.4x category won.
playbooks.check: Give refunds time to come in. Use orders at least 45 days old.

faq.q: What is return-adjusted ROAS?
faq.a: It is return on ad spend after you subtract refunded revenue. Ad platforms usually count the sale when it happens and never see the return, so their ROAS can look better than what you keep.

faq.q: Why use orders at least 45 days old?
faq.a: Returns arrive weeks after the order. If you include recent orders, many refunds have not happened yet, and every category looks better than it really is.

faq.q: Should I stop advertising high-return categories?
faq.a: Not straight away. First lower spend in steps and fix the cause of returns, such as unclear sizing. If net ROAS stays weak after that, cut further.

faq.q: Do I need Claude for this, or will any assistant work?
faq.a: Any assistant that can read your order, refund and ad spend data will work, including ChatGPT, Grok or Muse, from a connection or exported reports.

playbooks.title: Sell slow stock to likely buyers before discounting
playbooks.seo_title: Sell slow stock to past buyers before discounting
playbooks.meta_description: Find products with months of excess stock, match them to past buyers of the same style, and email that group before any markdown.
playbooks.hook: Before you mark down slow stock, email the people who bought that style before.
playbooks.answer: Before marking down slow stock, tell the people who bought that style before. Connect Shopify and Klaviyo, ask Claude to list products with more than six months of stock and the cash tied up, and find subscribed past buyers of the same style, color or category. Email that narrow group first, then discount only what is left.
playbooks.ask: List products with more than 6 months of stock at the current sales rate, with the cash tied up in each. For each, find past customers who bought the same style, colour or category, and how many are still subscribed.
playbooks.then: Email that narrow group first, at full price or a small offer. Discount only what's left.
steps: Connect Shopify and Klaviyo read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export inventory, orders and subscriber lists and upload them.
Ask the playbook prompt to list slow stock with cash tied up and the subscribed past buyers who match each product.
Check stock counts are current and that the products are not slow because of a fault or bad reviews.
Email the narrow segment first at full price or a small offer, holding back a slice to compare.
Count orders against the held-back slice, discount only what remains, and re-run each quarter.
playbooks.example: $40K sat in slow colours. A few thousand past buyers of that colour family had never been told.
playbooks.check: Send to a narrow segment first, and count orders against a held-back slice.

faq.q: How do I know which stock is slow?
faq.a: Divide units on hand by your recent sales rate. If it would take more than six months to sell at that pace, it is slow. Claude can do this per product from your inventory and orders.

faq.q: Why email past buyers before discounting?
faq.a: People who bought the same style or color already like it, so some will buy at full price. A markdown gives that margin away to everyone, including buyers who would have paid more.

faq.q: How do I measure whether the email worked?
faq.a: Hold back a random slice of the matched segment. Compare orders from those who got the email with those who did not over the same days.

faq.q: Can I use this prompt with Muse or ChatGPT?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can read your inventory, orders and email lists can run it, either connected to the tools or from files you export.

playbooks.title: Stop low-margin products eating Shopping spend
playbooks.seo_title: Stop low-margin products eating Google Shopping spend
playbooks.meta_description: Work out margin per product from Shopify costs, compare it with Google Shopping spend, and bid less on thin-margin products.
playbooks.hook: Your lowest-margin products may be taking the biggest share of your Shopping budget.
playbooks.answer: Low-margin products can take a large share of your Google Shopping budget. Connect Shopify, Google Ads and Merchant Center, ask Claude to work out margin per product after cost and shipping and compare it with each product's share of Shopping spend. Label products by margin in your feed and bid less on the thin ones.
playbooks.ask: Using product cost in Shopify, work out the margin on each product after cost and shipping. Then show each product's share of Google Shopping spend for the last 90 days. Flag products with under 15% margin that take a large share of spend.
playbooks.then: Label products by margin in your feed and bid less on the thin ones.
steps: Connect Shopify, Google Ads and Merchant Center read-only through a Claude connector or MCP server, or export product costs and Shopping reports and upload them.
Ask the playbook prompt to work out margin per product and flag thin-margin products taking a large share of spend.
Check that product cost is filled in correctly in Shopify. Missing costs make the result guesswork.
Add a margin label in your feed and lower bids on thin-margin products in steps, with a review date.
Compare Shopping spend share and profit after the change with the prior period, and re-run each quarter.
playbooks.example: 22 products under 15% margin took 30% of Shopping spend.
playbooks.check: Product cost must be filled in correctly in Shopify, or this is guesswork.

faq.q: How do I label products by margin in Merchant Center?
faq.a: Use a custom label field in your product feed, for example high, mid and low margin. You can then split Shopping or Performance Max campaigns by that label and set different targets.

faq.q: What if my product costs are not in Shopify?
faq.a: Fill them in first, or supply a cost sheet. Without real costs, the margin math is a guess and may push budget the wrong way.

faq.q: Should I stop advertising low-margin products?
faq.a: Not always. Some bring in new customers who go on to buy more later. Lower bids first and watch total profit, not just Shopping return, before cutting further.

faq.q: Can ChatGPT or Grok run the same analysis?
faq.a: Yes. Any assistant that can read your product costs and Shopping spend can run this prompt, either through a connection or from exported product and campaign reports.
